FOREWORD
Luyia represents a bold experiment on the part of missionaries
in North Nyanza to evolve a single language from the numerous dialects
of the area. None of its supporters is unaware of the difficulties
attending such an experiment, but it is believed, and rightly
, that the number of local languages makes some such solution most
necessary for any sort of educational or Mission work.
It is clear that some languages, furthest removed from those of
the central area from which Luyia was constituted, will be - indeed
are - hostile to the new language, seeing in it a threat to their identity
. It may prove difficult to disarm such antagonism, but the
advantages of a single language will be made clearer if people are
willing to write in it, and if it proves possible to maintain a
steady flow of reading material. If Europeans can be persuaded to
learn the language so much the better.
This, they certainly will not do unless incentives and guidance
are forthcoming. The present contribution to Luyia grammar is, therefore
, to be heartily welcomed. Mrs. Donohew has built up at Kima, a
graded course in the language, which would arouse the envy of all
who have never had the benefit of systematic teaching in a vernacular.
This book is the outcome of those Courses, and the student may be
sure that difficulties encountered in learning the language for daily
communication will here be fully appreciated.
W. H. Whiteley.
E. A. S. I. R.

PREFACE
This book is the outgrowth of years of teaching Luyia. It has
not been written for the professional linguist, but for the many
laymen who need to have something in ordinary speech, which they can
grasp quickly and put to practical use in their work. As much as
possible Bantu technical terms, such as "Allamorphs, phonemes, vowel
harmonies," etc., etc., have been avoided.
Many people come to the Luyia area with no previous experience
in Bantu languages. For them it is too much to be plunged immediately
into the many noun classes with their many and separate sets of agreements
. Because of this only the person class (Class 1), which is
the most used and most irregular of all classes, is introduced, giving
its full set of agreements. Next, Class 2, which is completely regular
, is presented with its full set of agreements. By then the student
has gained a feel for the basic principles of the language, and
finds it easy to pick up the rest of the classes and their agreements.
Because of so many dialect differences numerous alternate forms
are given in parentheses in the hope that the student will be able to
find his way in his own dialect area.
It is regretted that there is so little about tone in the book.
But it is hoped that what is included will give the student some
idea of going ahead and getting the tone of the Luyia words.
There is a companion reader of graded reading materials to go
with the first part of this grammar. Its title is "First Course in
Luyia - A Graded Reader."
Acknowledgements
This book would not be complete without acknowledging my very
great indebtedness to many people who have given most generously of
their time and help during the preparation of the manuscript.
To Dr. W. H. Whiteley who has written the Foreword, I am most
grateful. Dr. Whiteley for a number of years has worked in connection
with the University of London. He has given unstintingly of his
time, helping to find the solutions to many problems which arose
during the time of research into the language.
My deep gratitude is also due Professor Desmond T. Cole, head
of the Department of Bantu Languages, of the University of Witwatersrand
, Johannesburg, S.A. for kindly looking over this MS
and giving me numbers of hours in conference. He gave many valuable
suggestions in ways of presentation. These suggestions have
been followed rather closely.
Also I am most grateful to the many Africans who have always
been ready to give information, and have been most encouraging
and appreciative. Special mention is due Mr. Frankson Okwemba,
Mary Wandera, Perusi Liabaya, and Rita Ayanga for the hundreds of
hours given during the gathering of sentences for the exercises,
also to many others from various tribes for checking on the exercises
.
To my colleague, Mr. Douglas E. Welch, I wish to express my great
thanks for writing in the phonetic characters for the letters and compounds
found under "Pronunciation" in the introduction.
June 15, 1962
G. D.

1. Luyia Alphabet:
A, B, Ch, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, Kh, L, M, Ñ̀, Ō, P, R, S, T, U,
W, Y, Ž.

2. Pronunciation:
a. Vowels: a, e, i, o, u are both long and short.
(1) Short vowels:
They are represented by the single written vowel,
bola - spoil (food); manya - know.
The initial vowel of all noun and adjective prefixes is
short.
eshichik̄ - spoon; inyama - meat.
(2) Long vowels:
(a) are represented by two identical letters and pronounced
in twice the length of time taken for one vowel.
boola - say, speak, talk; reeba - ask.
(b) All vowels preceding nasal compounds are long and need
not be doubled. Nasal compounds: mb, nd, ng, nj, and nz.
hends - worry; the ŋ is pronounced long.
lambs - whole; the ą is pronounced long.
(c) All vowels following w compounds, not monosyllabic or
end syllables, are long. Some w compounds: bw, kw, hw, lw,
kw, ndw, etc. Vowels following these are written short.
bwana - blow; the first ą is pronounced long.
ndwoluno - here it is; the first o is pronounced long.
(d) The initial vowel of vowel stem verbs, nouns, and adjectives
are all long, but written short.
(3) Pronunciation of vowels:
A (ą) like the ą in "father," but not so deep.
E (ę) like the ę in "say," without the final diphthong sound

Ch (χ) Palatal affricative. There is a difference in the way this ch is pronounced in Luyia and English. In Luyia it is like the ch in the soft German "ich;" chenda - travel.
D (d) appears only in combination with n; nd in pure Luyia. It is pronounced like d in English.
F (f) Labio-dental (also, some Baluyia make it a bilabial fricative). Like English f in "for;" fouba - throw away.
G (g) appears only in combination with n; ng. It is always hard as g in "got." The soft g as in "gentle" is represented by j.
H (h) Laryngeal fricative, as Cockney London "how." The true Luyia h is not aspirated as in English, though many educated Africans confuse the h in Luyia reading with the English h sound. But in normal speech they do not pronounce it that way. It is a voiced h, and because of this it is often not recognized in speech.
J (j) used only in combination with n; nj, unless in a few words of foreign origin as June, julia. It is like the j in "just" if a d were placed before it, dj. The j is spoken in the palate, not in the teeth as English.
K (k) Velar plosive, as c in "compare;" kana - tell a story.
Kh (x) Velar fricative, as ch in Scottish loch or the German koch or the Arabic kh in khallas. Khola - do, act.
L (l) Alveolar for the lateral l in "let;" lola - see.
L (l) Flapped. Many Baluyia have both the flapped l and the flapped r. Both are represented by j. If l is preceded by a, o, or u and is followed by j or e, the l becomes the flapped j. If an j or e precedes the l, it becomes the flapped r. To make the flapped l, the forward part of the tongue blade (not the end tip) is placed against the alveolar ridge, almost to the base of the upper front teeth, to make this sound.
To make the flapped r, place the tip end of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, making a sound like a very faint d.
For the flapped l sound listen to the way some Baluyia pronounce tsuli - early morning. For the flapped r listen to them pronounce shile - exceed. Some pronounce all theirs as flapped lle.
M (m) Bilabial nasal, as m in "man;" moola - crawl.
N (n) Alveolar, as n in "no;" nala - become accustomed.
Ng (ŋ) Velar nasal, "ing" in "singing;" ing'oma - drum.
Ny (ny) Palatal nasal, as ni in "onion;" manya - know.
P (p) Bilabial plosive, as p in "poor;" ppara - think.
R (r) Dental alveolar, always rolled as in the languages in Italy, Germany, etc.; re - put, place,appoint to
S (s) Alveolar fricative, as s in "so;" sama - sprinkle.
Sh (ʃ) Palato alveolar fricative, as ch in soft German "ich;" lishole-- frog
T (t) Alveolar plosive, similar to t as the British pronounce it in "pretty;" teema - try, test.
Ts (t) Alveolar affricative, as German z, or the ts in "its;" tsia - go.
W and Y are as in English "we" and "yet;" walli - you were;
yanza - like, love.
Z (z) Alveolar affricative is always in compound form with n; as nz in "MacKenzie."

d.Nasal Compounds:
A nasal compound is composed of a nasal consonant, m or n,
joined to another consonant which is formed with the same organs of speech. These forms belong together in one syllable.
One must listen carefully to a Muluyia pronounce these in order
to perfect one's own pronunciation.
Mb (m) Bilabial nasal compound, as mb in "embalm;" omulembe -
peace.
Nd (n,d) Dental alveolar nasal compound, as nd in "ended;"
endola - I see.
Nz (n,z) Dental and alveolar nasal compound, (nz is heard as nj
in some dialects) as nz in "Mackenzie;" inzofu - elephant.
Nj (n,j) Palato-alveolar nasal compound, as nj in "unjust" if a
d were placed before the j, as, "undjust;" enjenda -
I walk/travel.
Ng (ng) Velar nasal compound, The g is hard as in "get;"
ingubo - dress, garment.
Remember that all vowels coming before these nasal compounds
are pronounced long, but are written short unless because of
a principle called "long coalescence" to be studied later.
3. Vowel Sequence:
One very important set of vowel sequences which must be memorized
is that which is called "Coalescence." This is what happens to
a and another vowel following it. The two grow together in one
sound. The resulting sound may be long or short, depending upon
other principles of vowel sequence to be studied in this section.
Long Coalescence Short Coalescence
a + a = aa aba + ana = abaana a + a = a ba + abandu = babandu
a + e = ee aba + eka = abeska a + e = e wa + ehale = wehale
a + i = ee aba + ibi = abeebi a + i = always long
a + o = oo aba + osi = abosisi a + o = o wa + omundu = womundu
a + u = oo aba + ula = aboola a + u = seems to be long only
General rules of vowel sequence follow.
When two vowels follow one another, a long or short vowel may result
:
a.Two similar vowels following one another resulting in a long
vowel sequence:
(1) Where the final vowel of an adjective prefix or noun class
prefix is the same as the initial vowel of the following
stem,both vowels remain, forming one long vowel.
ama + ani = amaani - strength
obu + uma = obuuma - forks
eshi + imbichiti = eshimibichiti - a short (thing)
shi + ina? = shiina? - what
(2) Where the final vowel of an infinitive prefix, or of a subject
, object, tense, or other prefix is the same as the initial
vowel of the stem immediately following, both vowels
remain, forming long vowel sequence,
okhu + ula = okhuula - to arrive
ka + amanga = kaamanga - They are bearing fruit.
a + ka + aya = akasye - He herds them.
a + shi + ibanga = ashiibanga - He is still stealing.
a + ku + usia = akuusia - He causes them to arrive.
ku + umanga = kuumanga - It is drying.
ka + la + ana = kalaana - They will bleat.
b.Two dissimilar vowels, one following the other, may result in
long or short vowel sequence. When the first vowel is a, this a
and the following vowel grow together into one sound (Coales-

body_text:
cence as given above):which may be either long or short.
(1) Long vowel sequence or coalescence.
(a)See tables of coalescence above.
(b)A final a of a prefix in combined forms with ifwe,
inyve, ifu, inyu,-ina?,-inj, and other pure i stems
coalesce long.
wa + ifwe/ifu = weefwe/weefu - our
na + inyve/nyu = neenywe - and/b/with you.
nina + inywe = nineenywe - and/b/with you
ba + ina? = beena? - who? whom?
sa + ifwe = seefwe - our father
khulwx + inywe = khulweenywe - for your sakes
(c)The possessive particle always ends in a, and when it
is prefixed to a demonstrative pronoun beginning with
a vowel (except one beginning with u), it forms long
vowel sequence or long coalescence. If the demonstrative
begins with a u, a w glide goes before it and no
coalescence takes place.
wa + uno = wawuno; ba + ulia + bewulia.
kwa + okwo = kwokwo; wa + eshio = weeshio.
(d)Other words or particles ending in a follow this same
principle of long coalescence. Example: na.
na + oyo = nooyo; na + abo = maabo.
(2) Short vowel sequence of a or short coalescence.
(a) The a of the possessive particle, when prefixed to
nouns, adjectives, infinitives, adverbs,locatives,
etc., forms short vowel sequence or short coalescence.
The resulting single vowel is spoken on a high tone,
wa + omundu = womundu; tsai + emisasa = tsenisasa
shia + (e)imusi = shtembusi; bia + okhuranga = biokhuranga
; ba + ehale = behale.
(b) The a of ne- - and/with/b/when joined to a following
noun, adjective, infinitive, adverb, or locative,etc.,
forms short vowel sequence or coalescence. The resulting
short vowel is spoken on a high tone.
na + omwana = nomwana; na + omulayi = nomulayi; na +
okhumanya = nokhumanya; na + elwanyi = nelwanyi.
(c) The a of the na- prefix of the near future tense before
an e, o and a form short coalescence. But this
same na- before 2nd person subject prefix u does not
change; both vowels remain.
na + ekhole = nekhole; na + olole = nolole; na +
atsie = natsie. There is no special tone for these
remaining vowels.
but -
na + ukhoonye = naukhoonye.
(3) The i of ni copula, coming before a word beginning with a
vowel, seems to drop out, forming short vowel sequence.
There is no special tone for the remaining short vowel.
ni + omwana = nomwana; ni + eshindu = neshindu; ni +
ifwe = nifwe.
c. Two dissimilar vowels both remain.
a + shi + ekanga = ashiekanga; ba + shi + ulanga = bashiulanga
; na + undole = naundole; ni + uninda = niuninda.
d. Vowel sequence between words:
The vowel at the end of a word seems to disappear in pronunciation
before an initial vowel of a following word.

Written Like This Pronounced Like This
shinga olwa (obwa) shingolwa (shingobwa)
ne olwa nolwa
ne abandu nabandu
khulwa okhutsia khulwokhutsia
šía omukhási shiomukhasi
šía (e)inyanga shiesinyanga
ali okhutsia alokhutsia
navule orie? nawulorie?

4. Consonant Sequence.
Nasalization is the term applied to this sequence. When n comes
before a consonant, something always happens; either the n drops
out entirely, the two form another set of letters, or they form
a compound nasal. This n always appears in a prefix: subject,
object, noun, or adjective. Before consonant stems these prefixes
are en-, in-, tsin-, or nin-. But if these prefixes are followed
by a vowel stem, the following things happen. If an n or
m follow the vowel of the stem, a y is added to the prefixes, giving
any-; iny-, tsiny-, ny-. If the vowel is the reflexive pronoun
i or iy, a d is added to these prefixes, giving end-, ind-,
tsind-, nd-. For all other vowels following the prefixes add a
z, giving enz-, inz-, tsinz-, and nz-. The following list shows
the nasalization which takes place when these prefixes are followed
by another consonant. See page 65 for special treatment of
these prefixes,
n + p or n + b = mb. Sometimes n + h = mb, or n may drop out before
hi peara - think = embara - I think,
bala - count = elbala I count.
harfa - light = embarfa, or ehafia - I
light.
n + t or n + l = nd. Sometimes n + r = nd, or n may drop out before
ri teekha - cook = endekha - I cook.
lole - see = andola - I see.
But if n or m follow in the next syllable after l,
the n + l = nd but the d drops out.
lima - dig = enima - I dig,
reeba - ask = endeeba, or ereeba - I ask,
n + k = nk.
kwa - fall = engwa - I fall.
än + kali = ingeli - large, big.
n + ts = nz.
tsia - go = enzia - I go.
n + ch = nj.
chenda - travel = enjenda - I travel.
n + y occasionally = nz. in + yokha = inzokha - snake.
n + yabila = nzabila - Bury me.
n + n, m, s, y, f, w, kh, sh, and many times before r and h drops
out.
5. Syllables:
Luyia has no closed syllables, i.e., no syllable ends with a consonant
. Every syllable must end with a vowel. Be careful not to
pronounce the first consonant of a following syllable with the
last vowel of a syllable. This makes for faulty pronunciation. If
a word must be divided, as at the end of a line, be sure to put
the hyphen after the last vowel, not after a consonant or between
a long vowel of two similar letters. An ia combination is treated
as a diphthong and belongs in one syllable.
e - mi - le - mbe = peace; o - mu - tee - shi = a cook; o - mu -
sia - ni = boy; o - khu - che - nda = travel; o - mwi - bi = thief.
6. Stress:
Stress has no significant function in Luyia. Words or syllables
are either spoken short or long, or on high, low, or medium tones.
To a foreigner this often gives the impression of stress. When the
possessive particle or na- conjunctive are joined to following
nouns or adjectives, the a disappears but the remaining vowel is
spoken on a high tone, which to some appears to be stress. When a

k. The na- conjunctive is to be joined to the following word; the capital, if there is one, comes at its usual place. Short coalescence takes place when it is joined to a following noun, adjective, infinitive, etc., and the remaining vowel is spoken on a high tone.
nOtieno - and Otieno
NOTieno (at the beginning of a sentence)
nomukhasi - and a woman
1. Ne - but/and is always written separately, but if it is before a word beginning with a vowel, the e disappears in pronunciation.
ne omanye mbu - but/and that you may know (pronounced as if written nomanye mbu.
m. General Note: Possessive particles, locatives, na- conjunctive, and ni copula, when they come immediately before a proper noun, the proper noun is to be written with its capital at its usual place, and short coalescence takes place in joining these particles.
eshitabo shiOluluyia - a Luyia book
omuruchi waBayahudi - ruler of the Jews
omundu weButere - a Butere person
Kalukhasia muLusungu - translate into English.
Rita nAyote nende Oycle - Rita and Ayote and Oycle
Niwina? NOTieno. - Who is it? It is Otieno.
9. Palatalization:
When the letters i or e follow k, kh, or ng, the spelling changes in the following manner: k + i/e = ch; kh + i/e = sh; ng + i/e = n.
k becomes ch: khalaka becomes omukhalach, akhalachila, ekhalasche,
kh " sh: bahka " omubashi, abashile, abasne
ng " ni: chinga " omuchini, achinile, achinje
10. Parts of Speech:
There are seven fundamental parts of speech in Luyia. These may be subdivided according to the particular form which the words may take, and according to their specific significance.
1. Substantive: a. Noun (divided into 14 classes)
b. Pronoun (1) absolute (7 uses)
(2) demonstrative
(3) enumerative
(4) qualificative
2. Qualificative:a. Adjective
b. Relative
c. Numeral
d. Possessive
3. Predicative: a. Verb (1) Regular dissyllabic
(2) Irregular dissyllabic
(3) Monosyllabic
(4) Polysyllabic
(5) Vowel stem
(6) Derivative
b. Copulative"ni"
4. Descriptive a. Adverb
b. Ideophone
5. Conjunction
6. Interjection (including vocatives and imperatives)
This classification is adapted from that of C. M. Doke.
11. Greetings and Useful Expressions:
Bushieele! = Good morning! (lit. It has become light).
Mulembe - Hello (to one person; lit. peace)
Milembe - Hello (to more than one person)

Bwakheels, or Bwilele - Good afternoon/evening.
Oli orie? - How are you (sing.)?
Muli murie? - How are you (pl.)?
Endi/khuli bulayi. - I am/we are all right.
Mbula iwe/nywe? - And perhaps you?
Oli omulamu? - Are you (s.) well?
Muli abalamu? - Are you (pl.) well?
Es, endi/khuli omulamu/abslamu. - Yes, I am/we are well.
Often the answer is Ahale or A-m, which means "nothing to complain of."
Akomutsuli/akomukamba? - What is the news of the morning?
Akeshiteere/akomubasu? - What is the noontime news?
Akobwile/Akomukolooba? - What is the evening news?
Orulile heena?/Murulile heena? - Where have you (s. and pl.)
come from?
Otsia heena?/Mutsia heena? - Where are you (s. and pl.) going?
Enzia/knutsia - I am/we are going...
Nave otsie heena?/Nenyewe mutsia heena? - And where are you going?
Orio (embwo). - Thank you (to one). Murio. - Thank you (pl.).
Olindwe. - Goodbye (to one). Mulindwe. - Goodbye (pl.).
Shiesia abeingo. - Greet those at home for me.
12, Explanations of Abbreviations used in the Patterns in this book.
SP = subject prefix
VR = verb root
VS = verb stem
IV = initial vowel
PP = possessive particle
DRP = direct relative particle
IRP = indirect relative particle
AP = absolute pronoun
OP = object prefix
NP = noun prefix
Ad.P = adjective prefix
Ad.S = adjective stem
Pad = possessive adjective
BVR = basic verb root
Ad.VR = applied verb root
RVR = reciprocal verb root
PVS = passive verb stem
NOf = number prefix
NOb = number stem
PC = pronominal concord
Plus signs: It will be noted that all patterns given in this
book have plus (+) signs. They are used in two ways. Those on
a line with the other parts of the pattern indicate that all
those parts are to be combined in one word. But the raised plus
indicates that what follows is separate from the foregoing pattern.
SP + OP + VR + a : All this goes together in one word;
but,
Shi + SP + VR + a + tawe : All the first part goes together to
make up one word, but the tawe following the raised plus is a
separate word.

Luyia has no definite or indefinite articles.
Questions
The word order is the same as for a statement with voice inflection for a question. The question may add such words as nohomba?, noho?, Shikali kario (mbwo)?, tse?, or mba? - "Is it not so?"
Interrogatives such as wina?, shina?, heera?, etc. come at the end usually.
Infinitives
Infinitives are formed by prefixing okhu- to the verb stem. The u changes to w before unlike vowels. If a following vowel is u both u's remain. Infinitives are also used as nouns or gerund nouns, but not as participles.
Na- joins to the following word always. It forms long coalescence with ifwe -we, us; inwe - "you" (pl.); and with all demonstratives beginning with a vowel except u. It forms short coalescence with all other words beginning with vowels. The coalesced vowel is spoken on a relatively high tone.
Na- with demonstratives beginning with u has a w between.
nomukhasi
nooyo
naabo
nawuno

and/with/by that one
and/with/by those
and/with/by this one
Na- and nende join infinitives, compound subjects, and compound objects. Nende is used before the last word of the series. The others may use na-.
Omukhasi nomukhaana nende omusiani balhio.
Uno nooyo nawulia nende bano

to see and to count and to ask, or, seeing and counting and asking
Both na- and nende express "and," "with," and, with the passive forms, "by."
With proper nouns na- is joined, the noun retaining the capital letter. It coalesces short with those beginning with vowels.

Uno is immediately near, within reach of the speaker, or closer than to the one
spoken to. Bano is the same. Uyia and yaba are relatively near or equidistant
with each speaker. Uria and bala are away from both speakers.

Exercise 1
Kalukhasia muLusungu (Translate into English):
1. okhuboola bulayi. 2. okhuboolela halala nende abassata. 3. okhumenya bulayi. 4. okhuteekha halala nende omukhara nomukhasi nende abana. 5. okhulola abantu bano. 6. okhubala abakhasi nende abana yabo. 7. Okhukhola bubili. 8. okhureeka omundu. 9. okhumenya ingo halala nabasiani yabo makhehana nawanyenende omusata. 10. okhuteekha rawini? okhuteekha mayabo. 11. okhukhoonya beena? 12. okhuboolela omundu okhukhoonya. 13. okhuteekha hatiiti bulsano.
Exercise 2
Kalukhasia muLuyia (Translate into Luyia):
1. to speak well. 2. to converse together with the men. 3. to live well. 4. to cook together with a girl and a woman and children. 5. to see these people (by me). 6. to count the women and these children (equidistant between you and me, or as far from us as you and I are from each other - not too far). 7. to do badly. 8. to ask a person. 9. to live at home together with those boys (near you) and girls and this one (all equidistant from each other) and a man. 10. to cook with whom? to cook with those (by you). 11. to help whom (pl.). 12. to tell the person to help. 13. to cook a little now.
Verbs in the Present Tense
All Luyia verbs have roots. When -a is added to the root, except the verb li -am, is, are, "we" have the present indicative stem. Lol- is the root of "see." If we add -a-, we have the present tense verb stem lola.
Abbreviations: VR = verb root; VS = verb stem. These abbreviations will be used in the future lessons. See p. xvii in Introduction for explanation of abbreviations.
In English we say, "The man sees!"; "The cow eats." In Luyia we say, "The man he sees"; "The cow she eats." The pronouns "he" and "she" are subject prefixes in Luyia and must be prefixed to the verb stem. Since for awhile we shall study only about people, we shall now learn only the person subject prefixes. Later we shall learn the subject prefixes for "it" and "they" for things. The following are subject prefixes for verbs beginning with consonants, called consonant stems.
Singular Plural
1st Person en- - I khu- - we
2nd Person o- - you mu- - you
3rd Person a- - he/she (not "it") be- - they (not of things)
Let us conjugate emenya - "lives." The rules in the Introduction under "Nasali- zation" apply to the conjugation of verbs also. Note that n drops out before m. Thus in the 1st Person singular n is elided, leaving only e-. This gives emenya - "I live." Pattern 5 P + VR + n = Subject Prefix + Verb Root + a
Singular Plural
1st Person emenya - I live khumenya - we live
2nd Person omenya - you live mumenya - you live
3rd Person amenya - he/she lives bamenya - they live
The stems -pi = "thus, in this way"; -rio = "how?" and -rio = "like that, in that way" all use these subject prefixes thus, endi, ori, ari, khuri, mari, bari, endie? orie? arie? khurie? mariie? barie?; endio, orio, ario, khurio, murio, bario.
Exercise 3
Kalukhasia mulusungu:
1. Endola omwana. 2. Enyala okhuteekha bulayi. 3. Okhooonya omishie. 4. Mubala abandu. 5. Omunya heera? 6. Endi omukhara. 7. Oli omukhasi. 8. Endesha bulano. 9. Khuresta abandu. 10. Abasiani bgola abana. 11. Abashiele baooleelana halala. 12. Oryala okhukhoonya abashiele bulayi. 13. Abana bakhola bubili. 14. Omundu uno areeba omusiani uyo (or, oyo). 15. Omukhasi uyo akhoo- nya omukhasi ulia. 16. Abantu yabo banya okhubeekha halala nende yabo (or, abo). 17. Omukhasi uyo (or, abetaa) bala banya okhuteekha halala nende yabo (or, abo). 18. Omwana ulia areeba balia. 19. Aba- lina (or, abetaa) bala banya okhuteekha halala nende yabo (or, abo). 20. Omundu anyala okhukhola bulayi, nomchwa anyala okhukhola bubili. 21. Abakhaye yabo bemena bulayi. 22. Omunya mano, nomomba? Tawe, emenya halia. 23. Aba- siani balino, nomomba? Ee, balino. 24. Abasiani bali heem? Balid yaho (or, aho). 25. Omukhasa akhooonya omushiele natiiti bulano. 26. Oli orie? Enyi bulayi. 27. Abakhama bali barie? (mbwena?) Rali bubili. 28. Omwana aboola ari (or, mbu). "Endola omusiani uno." 29. Abasiani bakhola barie (mbwena)? Rali khola bulayi. 30. Omundu uyo (or, oyo) okhole obubii.

2. The Indirect Relative Construction.
The indirect relative particles are own - whom (s.), and aba - whom (pl.). They are always written separately; the verb has another subject prefix. There are three uses of the indirect relative form. They are:
(a) the object of the relative clause.
Omussate, owe olola, amwenyange. - The man whom you see is smiling.
Abandu, aba ekhoonyanga, nabalele. - The people whom I am helping
long(in speaking) are sick.
Both these particles coalesce with an initial vowel in the following word, and the coalesced vowel is spoken on a high tone.
(b) for expressing "whom/which one has/is with," (see p.18),
(c) for expressing the possessive pronoun "whose" (see p.31).

> The relative Negative.
The re...ta/tawe negative is used with relative forms.
a.'Direct relative negative:
Pattern: DRP + ra + VS + ta/tawe
Abandu abarakholaa bulayi ta,mbabano. - The people who do not do do well are these.
b.'Indirect relative negative:
Pattern: IRP + SP + ra + VS + ta/tawe
Omundu,owa barakhoonya ta,nomalamu. - The man whom they do not help is well
Ta/tawe come at the end of the relative clause,unless the main clause is also negative,in which case one ta/tawe at the end of the sentence is sufficient.

Object Prefixes
In Luyia the pronoun objects "me, you, him, her, us, them" are represented by particles called object prefixes (OP), so called because they are always prefixed directly to the verb stem. Some are given here.
Singular
Plural
-n-, -ny-, -nz-, -nd- = me
-khu- = us
-mu- = you
-mu- = him, her
-ba- = them
Pattern: SP + OP + VS
Embalola bulayi. - I see them well. (Nasalization still takes place.)
Object prefixes for "me:"
a. before consonants:
Pattern: SP + n + VS (n nasalizes). Bandola. - They see me.
b. before vowels, followed by n or m:
Pattern: SP + ny + VS Banyenya. - They want me.
c. before reflexive i:
Pattern: SP + nd + VS Bandikomba muno leelo. - They desire me very much today.
d. before all other vowels:
Pattern: SP + nz + VS Banzitsila. - They come to me.
When the object prefixes -khu- and -mu- are used, it is not always clear whether "you, him, her, or us" is intended. To make this clear the absolute pronouns are used.
Ekholola iwe. - I see you.
Amulola inywe. - She sees you.

Object Prefix "me"
The use of the object prefix "me" is governed by four things.
1.All the rules of nasalization apply to its use when the object prefix
is n. Where n is elided, if there is any ambiguity of meaning, an apostrophe
is to be used in its place. See the Introduction under "Nasalization
," page xiv. Ya'khoonya kha. - He helped me long ago.
2.When the object prefix for "me" follows the subject prefix for "he/she;",
the subject prefix becomes ya. Thus for past tenses an apostrophe is
often needed to make the meaning clear.
Yamboola. - He tells me.
Ya'khoonyanya. - She used to help me.(This will not always be needed.)
3.When the object prefix for "me" follows the 2nd person singular "you,"
the subject prefix becomes u.
Undola. - You see me.
Ukhoonyanya. - You are helping me.
When any object prefix is used with an infinitive, it is spoken on a high
tone. Khunyala okhumulola. - We are able to see him/her.

Object Prefix With Commands
With all object prefixes except "me" one form is used.
Pattern: O P + V S in the subjunctive mood.
Bakhoonye. - Help them.
Muroobe. Ask him/her.
With object prefix "me" either the imperative or subjunctive mood may be used.
Patterns for imperative mood:
Singular: O P + V R + a
Njinge. - Carry me (to one person).
Plural: O P + V R + e
Njinje. - Carry me (all of you).
Patterns for subjunctive mood: S P + O P + V R + e
Umboolole. - Tell me. (S P u is used for "you" singular when object prefix for "me" follows it directly.)
Mumboolole. - Tell me (all of you).
Exception: The subjunctive stem for ha, i.e., he, is always used, never the imperative.
Imperative: Mbe omwana. - Give me the child. (spoken to one or many).
Subjunctive: Umbe omwana. - (you s.) give me the child.
Mumbe omwana. - (you pl.) give me the child.
Omume omwana. - (You s.) give him/her the child.
Mubahe omwana. - (You pl.) give them the child.
Negative commands with the object prefix are always in the subjunctive.
Pattern: S P + ra + O P + V R + a + ta/tawe.
Oramukhupa ta. - Do not (s.) spank him. Muramukhupa ta. - Do not (pl.) spank him.

Conjugation of Vowel Stem Verbs
The subject prefixes:
Singular Plural
1st person enz-, eny-, end- - I khu-, khw- - we
2nd person w- - you mu-, mw- - you
3rd person ya- - he/she ba- - they
The prefix end- for "I" is used before the j-and jv of reflexive verbs. The khu- and mu- prefixes come before u vowels. Khw- and mw- come before unlike vowels. The prefixes ya- and ba- always coalesce long with vowel stem verbs. Whenever an ultimate i in a subject prefix, or an ultimate a, are followed with a like vowel both i's and a's remain.
Endiyosia. - I wash myself. *Enyena. - I want. *Enzitsa. - I come.
Khumabakha. - We build. Muulanga. - You are arriving.
Khwitsanga. - We are coming. Mvenya. - You want.
Yeekanga. - She is studying. Boombakhanga. - They are building.
Yaayanga. - He is herding. Baayanga. - They are herding.
* When the initial vowel of a vowel stem verb is followed by n or m, the subject prefix eny-, or enz- may be used for I, preferably eny-.
Enz- is used for all other vowel stem verbs which are not reflexives.
Singular itsa Plural
1st per. enzitsa - I come khwitsa - we come
2nd per. witsa - you come mwitsa - you come
3rd per. yeetsa - he/she comes beetsa - they come
osia
enzosia - I wash khwosia - we wash
wosia - you wash mwosia - you wash
yoosia - he/she washes boosia - they wash
The habitual or continuous of osia follows the pattern on page 3,for verbs ending in -ia. It is given below.
enzosinjia - I am washing khwosinjia - we are washing
wosinjia - you are washing mwosinjia - you are washing
yoosinjia - he/she is wash- boosinjia - they are washing
ing
The subjunctive ending is -njie. Some dialects use -iangie. But the first ending is Standard Luyia.
enzosinjie - let me be washing/I am to be washing, etc.
wosinjie - you may be washing/you are to be washing, etc.

Noun Substantives
The foundation of the Luyia sentence is the noun which forms the subject of the sentence. All the other parts of the sentence are brought into agreement with it.
Every noun consists of two parts, the stem and the prefix. The stem remains constant and is the main body of the word. The prefix determines whether the noun is singular or plural, and the class to which the noun belongs. In Luyia there are fourteen noun classes. Nine of these classes have singular an plural forms. The prefix of each is used to bring the words of the sentence into agreement. In this usage they are called concords or agreements. See the Table of Concords at the back of the book, page 182.
Class 1
omu - aba
The Person Class
All nouns in this class refer to human beings. They are formed as follows.
Prefix Stem Full Noun Meaning
Singular: omu - ndu omundu person
omu - lina omulina friend
Plural: aba- ndu abandu people
aba- lina abalina friends

Forming Nouns From Verbs
In Luyia one can take roots or stems of words and make nouns, verbs,
adjectives, adverbs, etc. There are two ways of forming nouns from verbs
in the person class. These are only general rules. There are exceptions.
1. Pattern:*'N P+V R+i denotes person or persons doing the act.
Verb Root becomes Singular Plural Meaning
khoi- work " omukholi abakholi worker(s)
lol- see " omuloli abaloli witness(es)
khoony- help " omukhoonyi abakhooonyi helper(s)
boh- tie, bind " ** omuboyi ababoyi binder(s)
ching- carry " omuchinji abachinji carrier(s)
teekh- cook, be ** omuteeshi abateeshi cook(s),
married to wife/wives
* N P = Noun Prefix. ** h+i = Ng+i or a = ni. Kh+i or a=sh. The rule about h is wrong. It should be h+i is pronounced as w. It is hoped this rule will be changed someday.
Exercise 17
Form singular and plural nouns from these verb roots to mean the doer(s)
of the act.
1.lilwats- preacher. 2.kamb- preacher. 3.ay- herdboy. 4.ibul- parent. 5.ib- thief. 6.ruk- ruler, king. 7.umbakh- builder 8. ek- pupil. 9.osi-- washer 10. am- chief, chief person
Exercise 18
Find the roots of the following word pairs.
1.omwatsi, abeelwatsi. 2.omukambi, abakambi. 3.omwayi, abayi. 4. omwibuli, abebuli. 5.omwibi, abeebi. 6.omuruchi, aberuchi. 7.omumba- shi, abombashi. 8.omwechi, abeechi. (i or e following k changes k to ch) 9.omwosii, abosii. 10. omwami, abami.
2. Pattern: N P+V R+a to denote person or persons acted upon.
Verb Root becomes Singular Plural Meaning
lol- see " omulole abalole one(s) seen
khoony- help " omukhoonye abakhooonye one(s) helped
boh- bind, tie, " omubohie ababohie prisoner(s)
imprison " omuchinji abachinji carrier(s)
Exercise 19

Exercise 20
Find the roots of the following word pairs.
1.omulole, abalole. 2.omukhoonye, abakhoonye. 3.omubohe, ababohe. 4. omulwale, abalwale. 5.omuchinje, abachinje. 6.omwibule, abeebule.
Noun Adjectives
Like the nouns, the Luyia adjective has two parts, the stem and the
prefix. The stem remains constant. The prefix agrees with the noun it
modifies, and, with few exceptions, is the same as the noun prefix. In
Luyia adjectives may also be nouns, but they still retain their adjectival
quality.
Word order: Buli and shia - "every" precede the nouns they modify. With
few exceptions(to be studied later) the first letter of a following noun
or adjective is elided when buli is used. Buli mundu, every person,
Shia coalesces in speaking with the initial vowel of a following
noun, but is written separately. The coalesced sound is spoken on a
high tone. Shia omundu -"every person"is spoken as if written shiomundu.

body_text:
- 27 -
All other adjectives follow the nouns they modify. Adjective prefixes
for this class are omu-, singular; and aba-, plural.
Formation of adjectives and adjectival expressions:
1. Pattern:AdP + Ad_S (Ad P = Adjective Prefix; Ad S = Adjective Stem)
omu- + lávi = omulayi - good, right, correct, nice (person)
aba- + rambi = abarambi - tall ones, tall people.
2. Pattern: * Poss. P + infinitive of verb for infinitive used as
an adjective. Short coalescence prevails, spoken on high tone.
omundi wokhukhoonya - the person to help (lit. person of to help).
Omundu wokhureeba niyohana. - The person to ask is John.
* Poss. P = Possessive Particle. In person class these are wa- = "of"
for the singular, and ba- = "of" for the plural.
3. Pattern: P P + adverb or demonstrative of place.
omundi wahano - a local person. (lit. a person of here.)
Bano nabandu baKakamega. - These are Kakamega people.
There are not many pure adjective stems in Luyia. Khandi joins two
adjectives, or more, which modify the same noun.
Exercise 21
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Buli mwachi yasekanga butinyu. 2.Shia omufundi shiili nyokhumbakha
bulayi ta. 3.Buli mwibi nowaMaseno. 4.Shis omwechesia yesechesinjia bulayi.
5.Omwan omulayi nukhoonyanga bulayi. 6.Abandu abalayi nibo abamanyaga bulayi.
7.Omusekhubu uyo nomundu wokhureeba. 8.Omwan omulayi nomutsatsafahu.
9.Omundu uyo nomwimbichiti khandi nomnyelele. 10.Omukhaye ulia nomukooisi. 11.Abeechi yabo nababii. (The ni copula is used
before adjectives in the 3rd person instead of the full verb "to be.")
12.Omwan uyo yeeyena okhuyiciosa dze omulafu. 13.Abandu abatiti shibali abakali ta. 14.Omundu uyo nomukuraka; shyeeyena okhuyinzila ta. 15.Omurambi shiili omwimbichiti ta. 16.Abeechi abachesi shibali abasilu tawe.
17.Omwami ulia nomukhonga khandi omulayi.
Exercise 22
Kalukhasia muLuluya:
1.Every pupil is studying hard. 2.Every fundi is not one who is able to
build well. 3.Every thief is a Maseno person. 4.Every teacher is teaching
well. 5.A good child, is one who helps well. 6.Good people are they
who live right. 7.That old man is the person to ask. 8.A good child is
happy. 9.That person is short and slender. 10.That woman yonder is gracious.
11.Those pupils are bad. 12.That child wants to wash himself so
that he may be clean. 13.Small people are not large. 14.This person is
lazy; he does not want to work. 15.A tall person is not short. 16.Clever
pupils are not stupid. 17.That chief yonder is great and good.
Comparison of Adjectives
Luyia adjectives do not have degrees of comparison. The adjective itself never changes. If the idea of comparison is needed, the verbs
okhushila and okhuyomba - "to exceed" are used. Often muno or okhushila
muno are used following the adjective. Sometimes mu- - "among, of, in"
is used in certain combinations. Some common expressions are here given.
1.Luka nomulayi, nebutswa Yohana
amushile.
2.Yohana nomulayi okhushila Luka.
3.Luka naPaulo nende Yohana nabalayi
, nebutswa Asa nomulayi
okhushila bosii.
4.Niye omulayi okhuyomba bosii.
5.Okwamba niye ouchilanga bosii
mubulayi.
6.Mubosi Okwamba niye omulayi.
7.Yohana ashila Luka mubulayi.
Luke is good, but John is better
(exceeds him).
John is better than Luke (is good
to exceed Luke).
Luke and Paul and John are good, but
Arthur is the best (is good to
exceed them all).
He is the best of all (is good to
exceed all).
Okwamba is the best of all (it is
he who exceeds all in goodness).
Among of them all Okwamba is the
best (is the good one).
John is better than Luke (exceeds
Luke in goodness.)

9.Seruya akhoonya bulayi, ne Lea akhoonya bulayi muno.

For expressing "most" the verbs shila or yomba are used together with obunjì or obvinjì - "quantity, muchness" in relative construction.
1.Abeebuli, abashila obunjì, bali na-bana abslayi.
2.Abakhana, abayomba obunjì, balima-nza.
3.Abasiani, abashila obunjì, baaya-nza bulayi.
In making expressions equivalent to the comparison of adjectives using shila or yomba, the adjective must be present. Otherwise, it will be an adverbial expression.

Exercise 24
Kalukhasia muLuluya:
1. This herdboy is bad, but that one is worse. 2. Dishon is worse than Olubaya. 3. This child is small, but that one is smaller than he. 4. Andele is short, and Mucheni is short, but Otundo is shorter than them all. 5. That one is difficult, and this one is more difficult than that one, but that one yonder is the most difficult of all. 6. Saayi is fatter than Timothy. 7. Of all Rita's children Otundo is the slenderest (the slender one). 8. Those yonder are better than those (exceed those in goodness). 9. Most teachers teach well. 10. Most chiefs rule well. 11. That person is mean, but that one yonder is meaner (very mean).
Object Prefixes With Vowel Stems
1. General rules.
a. Pattern: u of O P remains before another u. (O P = Object Prefix).
Bamumbashilanga. - They are building for him.
b. Pattern: u of O P becomes w before unlike vowels.
Bakhwosinjia. - They are washing us.
Amwitsila. - He comes to her.
c. Pattern: a of O P + a of V S = ae.
Omwami abasyanga bulayi. - The chief cares for them well.
d. Pattern: i of O P + i of V S = ii.
Ashiibile. - He stole it (shi for "it - the thing").
2. Object prefix "me."
a. Pattern: ny + vowel + n or m.
Banyenya. - They want me.
b. Pattern: nz + vowel not followed by n or m.
Unzecheshinjia. - You (s,) are teaching me,
Yanzitoklanga. - She is coming to me.
c. Pattern: nd + reflexive verb stem - Bandikomba. - They want me.

3.Omwechesia wabeechi bano abezechesinja bulayi khatstoto. 4.Omwibaliile okhuteekha. 5.Omukhasi uyo yanzibaalilanga okhusinga abaana. 6.Unyenyaa.
7.Abeana nabamali; né.omukhasana aboosinjia babe abalafu. 8.Omwami yanye-nya? Yee, akhwenya. 9.Abeana bali heena? Omwechesia uno abeenya. 10. Abandu bomwami uyo nabatsatsahafu, shichila abaayange bulayi. 11. Ulia nomwechi, ne uyo amwechesinja butinyu. 12.Abeebuli bano bali nabana baraano ababeenyangana muno. 13.Omwechi akhwenya ifwe. 14.Omwami akhwenya iwe bwangu. Akhulanganga.
Exercise 26
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.You (s.) are teaching me well. 2.That teacher does not teach me badly. 3.The teacher of these pupils always teaches them well. 4.Teach me cooking/to cook. 5.The woman is teaching me to bathe babies. 6.Do you (s.) want me? 7.The children are dirty, and the girl is washing them. 8.Does the chief want me? Yes, he wants you. 9.Where are the children? This teacher wants them. 10.This chief's people are happy because he shepherds them well. 11.That one yonder is a pupil, and that one is teaching him hard (diligently). 12.These parents have five children who are wanting them. 13.The pupil wants us. 14.The chief wants you quickly.
He is calling you.
Reflexive Verbs
Reflexive verbs express "self" and "-selves," as, "myself," "himself," etc.
1. They are formed in two ways.
Pattern a: i + consonant V S.
ireeba - ask oneself.
iruke - control oneself.
Pattern b: iy + vowel stem verb.
iyosia + wash oneself.
iyefesia - teach oneself.
The i and iy are object prefixes, so they do not change a dissyllabic to polysyllabic, or a monosyllabic verb to dissyllabic. These reflexive verbs take the subjunctive stems for all commands;Yireebe omwene.
2. Subject prefixes for reflexive verbs:
a. for "i" is end- usually, and end- for object prefix "ms."
b. All other subject prefixes are the same as for vowel stem verbs.
In this class omwene and abeene are often used after these verbs for emphasis or clarity.
Endiyosinjia omwene. - I am washing myself (arms, legs, head).
Wireebe omwene. - Ask yourself.
Exercise 27
Kalukhasia muLusungu:

Abana beesinga (beeyosia) bulano. 4.Abasyi beeyosinjia halia khatstoto. 5.Omutofu nomundu ooreerukanga bulayi tawe. 6.Omundu anyala okhwiyochesia omwene okhuteekha. 7.Abana yeba nabakali; banyela okhwiwala abeene bulayi. 8.Omundu omulayi yeereebanga omwene mbu, "Exholanga bulayi khatstoto?" 9.Enyenyaa (or, enzenyaa) okhiyosia omwene. 10.Abana yabo beebobanga abeene. 11.Omundu omukosi yeerukaanga omwene bulayi.
Exercise 28

teema - try, attempt, tempt, test
omutukitarri + doctor
abatukitarri - doctors
omulesi, omasilishi - one who
tends or treats the sick
abalesi, abasilishi - nurses, doctors
daktari - doctor (direct address)
*henga. In some dialects words beginning with han- or hen- nasalize to
mb and the b drops out. Henga is a case in point. Thus some people say,
"Emenganga" instead of "Ehenganga" or "Embenganga."
Possessive Adjectives
Pattern: P.P + 'A.P
Some of the alternate absolute pronouns are used in forming possessive
adjectives. See p. 13 for the alternate forms.
To understand the structure of possessive adjectives, remember always
the literal translation.
wa- + -nje = wanje - of me, my,
wa- + -bo/-bwe = wabo/wabwe - of them, their
The possessive adjective follows the noun it modifies and agrees with
it in number.
omwana wanje - the child of me, my child
abana banje - the children of me, my children
The second and third persons singular have short and long forms. The
short forms join the preceding noun as a suffix; the long form is written
separately. The plural of the long forms, bobo and bebe are reduplications
, but not the singular forms. Some dialects vary in these
forms. An alternate variation is given in parentheses. The possessive
particles with these second and third person absolute pronouns, i.e.
u and e coalesce short, and they coalesce long with ifwe or ifu and
with inywe and inyu.

Following Singular Nouns

3rd per. wa- -e -we,wuwe, of him/her (uwe) his/her
Plural
PP A P P Ad. Meaning
wa - ifwe, weefwe, of us, our
ifu weefu
wa- inywe, weenywe, of you, inyu weenyu your
wa- bo, wabo, of them, wa- bwe wabwe their,

1.Seven trees are tall and all the others are short. 2.Sixteen ropes are about to be bought, but the other four have not yet been braided. 3.One year can be good, and another one can be bad. 4.One boy is fat, and the other one is slender. 5.Two people are eating, and all the others are digging. 6.Some months are longer than others. 7.Eighty-eight ropes are being braided, but those others not yet (have not yet been braided). 8.Forty-two blankets are still to be bought, and these fourteen are being bought now. 9.Two hundred and twelve people are here. 10.This person is thirty-five years old (lit., has thirty-five years).

Possessive Particles
The possessive particles for this class are: kwa- = of (sing.), and chia- = of (pl.). The same rules apply here as do for the possessive particles in the person class. See p. 10.

Exercise 3
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Omurwe kwaRita kusitothanga. 2.Omurwe kwomwana uyo nomukali. 3.Emirwe chisibana abanjì nemikali. 4.Omutoka kwomundu uyu nomulayi po! 5.Emisaala chibandu abanjì nemirambi. 6.Emikoye kwemwechi ula kubasungwa bulayi. 7.Emikoye emini chibandu nemitinyi (Note: If the possessive does not follow the noun it modifies directly, the initial vowel of the noun is prefixed to the possessive particle). 8.Omwana uno nowemiyika musane. 9.Omabayo kwomwana kube kuri, omulayi, khandi omutsatsaharu. 10.Abasana bomukanda kuno nabemiyika musane. 11.Omusala kwomundu uyu nomululu po. 12.Omutoka kwEshitemi kwilukhanga po!

Exercise 6.

The ropes of these groups of children are long, but the ones of those are short. 9. The blankets of this group of children are large, and the ones of that one are also large. 10. The owners of these gardens are still digging, but the ones of those yonder are about to plant.
Object Prefixes
The object prefixes for this class are: -ku= it (sing.) and -chi= them (pl.). They are always prefixed to the verb stem; nothing ever comes between the two. The rules of nasalization apply as usual.

Omwilusi yeenyanga omutoka yikwo, nohomba? Ee, akwenya. 6. Wikale omulango. Engwikalanga bulaano. 7. Mwena okhikula emiliango chiosi? Ee, kwanya okhuchikikula chiosi. 8. Enyena oreme omusaala leelo. Enguremanga. 9. O! mubasanga emikoye. Ee, khuchibasanga. 10. Omwenemuseala yeenya mukureme, mana mukutonye.
Exercise 8
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1. The car is here; do you want it? Yes, I want it. 2. This blanket is large; do you see it? Yes, I see it. 3. Are you braiding ropes? Yes, I am braiding them. 4. Do you want to swallow this medicine? No, I do not want to swallow it. 5. Does the driver want that car? Yes, he wants it. 6. Close the door, I am closing it now. 7. Do you want to open all the doors? Yes, we want to open them all. 8. I want you to chop down the tree today. I am chopping it down, 9. Oh! you are braiding ropes; Yes, we are braiding them. 10. The owner of the tree wants you (pl.) to cut it down, and then cut it up in pieces.

header: The Applied Form of the Verb
body_text:
The applied form of the verb indicates action when applied on behalf of, towards or with regard to, an object. It expresses the idea of "with" when speaking of an instrument used for carrying out an activity, as "Cut the bread with this knife." When the applied form is used, intransitive verbs may become transitive, as Omukulushile. - You return to him. Transitive verbs in this form may take two objects. This form is often called the prepositional form. Locatives often cause a verb to take the applied form.
Ways of Forming the Applied Form
1. Monosyllabic verbs.
Group a: Pattern: V S + ila (long coalescence)
nywa + ila = nyweila - drink from/on behalf of
Group b: Pattern: V R + ila
tsi + ila = tsila - go to/for; go in or on an object
when locative is used
2. Verbs ending in -ia.
Pattern: V R + ila
osi + ila = osilia - wash for/with/in/on
3. All other verbs.
a. When the ultimate vowel of the verb root is a, i, or u:
Pattern: V R + ila
-kul + ila = kulila - by for; buy within the confines expressed by an accompanying locative.
b. When the ultimate vowel of the verb root is e or o:
Pattern: V R + ela
teekh~ + ela = teeshela - cook for; cook within the confines expressed by an accompanying locative.
4. There are also double applied forms which are used occasionally.
boola - say; boolela - tell, say to; boolelela - tell some one for a person.
Umboolelele Etindi yako. - Tell Etindi that for me.
Akhuteeshelelamwo. - She cooks for us in there.
Exercise 9
Kalukhasia mulisungi:
1.Omwa allenga, ne abaana bandi bamutesheelanga. 2.Lila omubano kuno. 3.Kulia nomutoka okwa khuchendelangamwo okhutsia Eshisumu. 4.Yikwo nomufukoo okwa omukhasi achinjilangamwo emikaate. 5.Ukhoonyele o-mulimo kuno. 6.Abendu balala bamenyela Nyasaye, abandi bamenyelanga eniandu. 7.Abendu yabo ba'rilangha shifina okhutsia Butere? 8.Omukhasi yeekulilang'omwere omukaate. 9.Mama abalila abandu mumutoka. 10.Undeshole; enenyanya okhulise. 11.Nzila khupapa, omubolele mbu, enenyanya. 12. Nyinamwana Luka ali Eshisumu niyeenyanga omukaate. Luka maye namukulililayo. 13.Omwilusi yanzilusilinjia omutoka. 14.Papa yanzarilanga omukunda. 15.Yeetselanga hano mumutoka khatsotso (The coalesced ee causes the applied ela to be used.). 16.Omwilwatsi (omukambi) yeelwatsilanga (akambilanga) abandu.
Exercise 10
Kalukhasia mululuya:
1.The child is crying, and the other children are laughing to him. 2. Eat with this knife. 3.That yonder is the car in which we travel to Kitumu. 4.That is the bag in which the woman carries bread. 5.eld / me with this work. 6.Some people live for God, others live for possessions. 7.Why are those people afraid for me to go to Butere? 8.The woman is buying herself some bread. 9.Mother counts the people in the car (she also is in the car). 10.Gook for me; I want to 'ask'. 11.Go to father for me and tell him I want him. 12.Luke's mother is in Kisumu, and wants some bread, and Luke buys (it) for her there. 13.The driver is driving the car for me. 14.Father is cutting furrows in the garden for me. 15.He always comes here in the car. 16.The preacher is preaching to the people.

Exercise 2
Kalukhasia mulisungu:
1. This car is simply terrible. 2. This car itself is good, but the driver is bad. 3. That sauce is delicious. 4. These blankets are terrible. 5. The head itself is large, but the mouth is small. (thin). 6. That one (person) is genuinely gracious. 7. These (people) are very wise. 8. The games of the children yonder are themselves good, but it is the children themselves who are playing badly. 9. This one (person) is able to cook marvellously well. 10. She nails are terribly long.
Relative Construction
1. The Direct Relative Construction
The direct relative particles for class 2 are oku- = which (s.), and echi- = which (pl.). They act in the same way as those in the person class. See p.16.
Exercise 3
Kalukhasia mulisungu:
1. Omotoka, okuli omusali, nokwajohana, ne okundi, okuli omulafu, nokwomusaatsa ulia. 2. Omurunjeti, okufvimbungwe omwana, nomusali. 3. Emirunjeti, echikhoonyanga abandu yabo, nechilomukhasi uyu. 4. Emtoka echishila obunjji, chililukhanga bulayi khumuhanda leelo. 5. Omahanda okuehanga elwanda, ngokuno, ne okuhenganga Kwiselo, ngwokulika. 6. Emihanda chiosi, echililanganga Nairobi, nemilayi. 7. Omwosi okutumangana leelo, nomunjji. 8. Omulembe, okuehebungwa abandu abeetsela Nyassaye, nomukhongo. 9. Omotoka, okuli omulayi, kunyela okhulukha bulayi, nebutswe okurali omulayi, shikunyala okhulukha bulayi tawe. 10. Emisasa, echikhulange bulayi, chitseza okhube emirimbi.
Exercise 4
Kalukhasia mululuyia:
1. The car which is black is John's, and the other one, which is white, is that man's yonder. 2. The blanket which covers the child, is dirty. 3. The blankets which are helping those people are this woman's. 4. Most cars run well on the road today. 5. The road which goes in the direction of Izwanda is this one, and the one which goes in the direction of Khwasero is that one yonder. 6. All roads which go in the direction of Malrob are good. 7. The smoke which is rising today is much. 8. The piece which is given to that people who come to God is great. 9. A car which is good is able to run well, but one which is not good is not able to run well. 10. The trees which are growing well are going to be tall.
2. The Indirect Relative Construction
The indirect relative particles are okwa = which (s.), and echia = which (pl.). They are the objects of relative clauses and are treated the same as those in the person class. See p. 17.
Exercise 5
Kalukhasia mulisungu:
1. Omotoka, okwa omufundi akasinja, nomubii muno. 2. Omahanda, okwa emitoka chichendangshiko, nomubambalifu (nomubambukhu). 3. Emitoka eminji, echia abeelsusi beelusinja, nemibi, ne echindi, echia abandi bareelu-sinja, shichili emibi ta. 4. Omushaara, okwa omundi uyu arunganga omukholiwe, nomutiti. 5. Emishaara, echia abeechesia bosi banyoolanga ha lala, neminji. 6. Omurunjeti okwa abandu bachamanga (bayanzanga), nomusiro. 7. Omwoyo, okwa abandu bachamanga (bayanzanga) okushila, nomutsatsahafu. 8. Omwesi, okwa abandu bachamanga okushila, nokwajune.
Exercise 6
Kalukhasia mululuyia:
1. The car which the fundi is fixing is very bad. 2. The road on which the cars are travelling are wide. 3. Many cars which drivers drive are bad, But others which others are not driving are not bad. 4. The salary which this man pays his workman is small. 5. The wages which all the teachers together receive are much. 6. The blanket (kind of blanket) which people like is a thick one. 7. The spirit which people like very much is the happy one. 8. The month which people like best is June.

Exercise 7
-Kalukhasia mulusungu:
1. Omukabo kwomuunyu, okwa oli ninakwo, nomunjì. 2. Emiyo, echia abandu abalayi bali ninachio, nemilayi, ne echia ababii bali ninachio, nemibì. 3. Onyala okhukula omurunjeti nende omushaera okwa oli ninakwo? 4. Omumumbashi anyala okhumusbakha bulayi-nende emisumari echia ali ninachio. 5. Emirunjeti chiosi, echia abeechi bali ninachio, chisambwe, shichila chiosi nemibì. 6. Emisugari chino nemilayi chiene, ne echia oli ninachio chiosi nemilayi. 7. Emifuko, echia muli ninachio, chili neminwa emikali, nebutswa echia yabo bali ninachio, chili nemititi. 8. Omuleme, okwa omundi anyala okhuba ninakwo, kunyala okhumukhola abe omutsatsahafu.
Exercise 8
-Kalukhasia mululuya:
1. The portion of sauce which you have is much. 2. The spirits which good people have are good, but the ones which bad ones have are bad. 3. Are you (s.) able to buy a blanket with the salary which you have? 4. The builder is able to build well with the nails which he has. 5. All the blankets which the pupils have are to be burned, because all of them are bad. 6. These nails are fine, and the ones which you (s.) have are also good. 7. The purses which you (pl.) have have large openings, but the ones which those have have small ones. 8. The peace which a person can have is able to make him happy.
Ordinal Numbers
Patterns:
1. for "first;" PP + mbeli or okhuranga
omundi wambeli - the first person; or okhuranga - the first one
2. for "second" through "sixth;" PP + kha + number stem
omutoka kwakhabili - the second car.
abandu bekharano - the fifth (group of) people
3. for all others: PP + number formed according to the above rules, or simply to the number itself.
omusnala kwelikhumi nakhabili - the twelfth tree
omukunda kwamunaane - the eighth garden
emisala chiamakhumi kabili nalulala - the twenty-first trees
*lulala is used for "first" after likhumi and amakhumi words, as "eleventh," "twenty-first," "thirty-first," etc.
When likhumi, imia, tsimia, tselefu, tsielefu, and imilioni are used, a pre-suffix e comes into play, as, omundi welikhumi - the tenth person.
If no noun precedes the number directly, the initial vowel of that noun is prefixed to the possessive particle, as, oweimia - the hundredth one.

Dates
For future or past dates the literal translation of Luyia is,"the month of So-and-so when it is such-and-such a number." "One" uses julaĩa, and "two" through "six" uses kha- with the number stem. The verb "to be" may be used for "at" times, or any past or future tense.

Reciprocal Form of the Verb
This derived form of the verb expresses the basic idea of "back and forth." One use is to express the idea of doing something to each other. Another use expressed mutual action in doing something, as in a relay race. It also is used for an act accompanying another action which has been planned, as, "You are going to visit uncle; take a long this bread to him."
This form does not use an object prefix. The words or particles na-, nin-, and nende are used to express the object.
Emboolelananga niayane. - I am talking with him.
This type is formed by fixing -an- between the verb root and ending.
1. Ways of forming the reciprocal form of the verb.
a. All verbs ending in -ia, except monosyllabic verbs, seem to have a basic root which ends with the last consonant of the normal verb root. This we shall call "the basic verb root (B V R)." The verb root (V R) ends with the i of the -ia ending.
Pattern: B V R + an + ia
Osia - wash becomes osania - wash each other. (gs + an + ia.)
Nyasia - trouble, torment becomes nyasania - trouble each other
b. All other verbs:
Pattern: V R + an + a
Kol + an + a, = lolana - see each other.
Thus it would seem that this -an- possesses all the properties required of an infix.

Because of the principle of vowel harmony in Luyia this -ilila ending coalesces and becomes -selela.
Group a:
Pattern: V S + ilel + an + a
khwa + ilel + an + a = khweelana - the process of getting a wife.
Group b:
Pattern: V R + ilil + an + a
kw + ilil + an + a = kwililana - become for each other.
3. All other verbs.
Pattern: Ap, V R + an + a
kholel + an + a = kholelana - do to/for each other.
limil + an + a = limilana - dig for each other.
The principal idea in these verbs seems to be much interaction over an extended period of time. There are other minor meanings.

People ought to pray for each other. 12. The boys are bringing each other knives. 13. Good friends go around together very much.
Applied from the Reciprocal Form.
Pattern: R V R* + ila (for all ve-ba ending in -la, except monosyllabic verbs).
Samban + ila = sambanila - burn each other with (something), or within the confines expressed by a locative.
* R V R = reciprocal verb root.
Pattern: B V R + ani + lia (for all verbs ending in -ia except monosyllabic verbs).
Os + ani + lia = osanilia - wash each other with/for or within confines expressed by a locative.
There are several meanings for this form.
1. Doing something to each other with an instrument.
Khakakanila emibano - cut each other with knives.
2. Doing something to each other within the confines expressed by a locative.
Khupanila mumutoka - beat each other in the car.
3. With the words yilarila and leeranila one is going for another purpose and he brings or takes along an object to someone or within the confines expressed by a locative.
Leeranila Mama omukatsa nivitsa - Bring along some bread to koether when you come.

For One's Sake/Part, On One's Account/Behalf, of One's Self/Power
There are two sets of expressions formed from khulwa- and khubwaon
the same pattern as possessive adjectives. Those formed from khulwadenote
for one's sake, for one's part, on one's account or behalf.
The khubwa- group indicate the idea of accomplishing something
through one's own strength or power.
khulwanwe, khululwo, khululwe, khulweefwe, khulweenywe, khulwabwe,
khulwakwo, khulwachio = for my part/sake; for your sake, on your
behalf, etc.; for his sake, on his account, on her behalf, etc.;
for our sakes; on our behalf, etc.
khubwenwe, khububwo, khububwe, khubweefwe, khubweenywe, khubwabwe
= of myself, of my own strength or power; of yourself, of your own
strength or power, etc.

Whose
Pattern: IRP + Noun + Pad.
Omundu owa omawawe - the person whose child (lit. the person whom the child of him).
Omukoka okwa omulango kwakwo - the car whose door.
The a of the relative particle coalesces with a following noun and is spoken on a high tone.

Abasana, aba emibano chiabwes chibahyāsinjia, balilanga.

Class 9
The Infinitive Class
Okhu
In Luyia infinitives form a noun class. These nouns seem to convey the idea of action in contrast to the state or condition portrayed by abstract nouns in the obu- class.

Class 10
A Locative Class
(a)ha habundu - place
There is only one pure noun belonging to this class. All others are formed from other nouns with this ha- locative prefix replacing the first letter of the original noun prefix, as, hamuliango - the place around the door. The normal prefix for this class is ha-, but if an initial vowel is needed for coalescence, etc. an a-preprefix comes into play. The ha- can be interpreted: the place near/round about/at.
Vocabulary
bukaana, akaana - meet with, meet bukaanila, akaanila - meet at/on/ each other with/for/in
tuya - bump into, pound tuyana - collide
habundu, handu - place hango - home place

Class II
A Locative Class
(o)ku
The general meaning of this class is "on." There are no nouns which
belong exclusively to this class. All are formed from other classes
by eliding the first letter of a noun prefix and prefixing khu-.
For plural nouns in this class, the agreements often are those of the
original noun in the plural. This can also happen to the singular
nouns. In these cases the noun would not be in the locative class.

Class 12
A Locative Class
(o)mu:
The meaning of this class is "in," "through." There seem to be no nouns native to this class. All are formed by prefixing mu- to other nouns. The first letter of a noun prefix is elided and the mu- is prefixed to the remainder of the noun prefix. Plural nouns often take the agreements of the original noun class, and occasionally of the singular noun form also. In such cases the nouns belong to their original class. The meaning for this class can be expressed as "the inside," the "inside place." An initial o comes into play when an initial vowel is needed. The adjective prefix is omu-.

Class 14
Locative Class of Distances
e-,i-,in- - (e)tsi-,tsinMeinhof
calls this the locative class of distances. The noun prefixes vary. Those given above are all which have been discovered so far. However, if vowel-stem nouns should be in this class, they would take the iny-, inx-,tsiny-, and tsin- and reflexive prefixes as in class 5 nouns. The adjective prefixes are synonymous with those of class 5. See page 63. The locative suffix for this class is -vo. There are some variations in the e- prefix. It is often superimposed upon another locative or another prefix. Some examples of these are ebu-,emu-, and ena-. Emukulu - the place on an incline above; enanzu - the place of a house; ebundu yilla - that place yonder. While demonstratives in the ha- and khu- classes usually indicate something which can be seen, the demonstratives in this class often refer to things some distance away and need not necessarily be seen. Nouns in this class are adverbial nouns of place. If the speaker is at his home, he can say, "Ingo/inzu yino neyanje. - This home/house is mine." But if he is some distance away from it, he would say, "Ingo/enanzu wanje yili ehale okhurulana hano. - My home is far from here." The first sentence uses class 5 nouns, the second, class 14 locative nouns.

Demonstratives of Reference
When one is referring to a person or thing about which one has been
talking, one usually uses the -ene form for"self"or"selves" followed
by a demonstrative. If the set of demonstratives beginning with vowele
are used, with the exception of those beginning with u, the final
e of -ene is dropped and the demonstrative is added as a suffix:
emwenoyo - that same one about which we have spoken; etsiensetsio -
those which.I have mentioned, etc. But with all other demonstratives
the -ene word is written separately: abene bano - these same ones;
obwene yibwo - that same one, etc.
Cardinal Numbers
The number prefix for 1 is the same as the adjective prefix minus
the initial vowel for all classes except class three. Class 3 uses
only the initial vowel prefixed to the -lala stem for 1, slala.
Class 5 uses the in- prefix, which minus the initial vowel is nThis
n- nasalizes the 1 to d, giving ndala for 1 in class 5. The
locative class khu- does not have a 1 belonging to it. The 1 is
in the class of the original noun class. The locative muclass
has
only 1 in it; any plurals revert to the plurals of the original noun
classes. Any noun in class 14 formed from another noun class takes
the plural of the original class of that noun. However, there are a
few nouns indigenous to this class, as indulo - edge, border. These
nouns would take the plural agreements of class 14.
The numbers 2 - 6 have the plural pronominal concord of the class
concerned prefixed to the number stems. All other numbers stand alone,
being complete without agreements. The numbers 11 - 19 follow the
combination 10 and 1, 10 and two, etc. All multiples of 10 are"tens
two, tens three, tens four," etc. - amakhumi kabilii = 20; amakhumi
kataru = 30, etc. The numbers 21 -n29, 31 - 39, etc. follow the same
pattern as 11 - 19, i.e., 20 and 1, 20 and 2, 30 and 3, etc., as,
amakhumi kabilii namulala, amakhumi kataru nelala, etc. The chart on
the following page shows the various patterns.
The number forms given in the chart are those agreed upon by the subcommittee
of the Luyia Orthography Committee for use in arithmetics.
1. Number one. Number Prefix = NoP; Number Stem = NoS;
Pattern: NoP + lala shilala = one (thing)

Immediate Past Tense of Verbs
There are nine primary verb tenses in Luyia: Present; immediate past, near past, intermediate past, and far past; immediate or Ja future, near or Na- future, intermediate or Kha- future, and the far or Li future. Each represents a different period of time, and within each time span of the past tenses there is a present perfect tense form. With the exception of the 3rd person singular and the far past tense, the difference is one of tone.

The immediate past tense is sometimes called the "just now" tense, because it indicates that something has just now happened. The time span is very limited.

The subject prefixes which we have been using up to now are called Type A subject prefixes. For this and some other tenses a set of prefixes called Type B are used. With the exception of the person class singular, an a is added to all Type A subject prefixes, except those which already end in a, to form Type B. The 3rd person singular uses wa- instead of ya- for the present perfect tense form. All present perfect forms have the a of the subject prefixes spoken on a lower tone, and the simple past is spoken on a higher tone, the higher tone being on the verb. When a is added to the ya- SP of class 5, the ya- drops out as usual. Although diacritical marks are not used in Standard Luyia, they will be used here to indicate the high tone of the present perfect tense as opposed to the lower tone of the simple past.

Relative Construction in Immediate Past
There are type A and type B direct particles just as there are type A and type B subject prefixes. They are formed by adding a to the direct relative particle, unless it already ends in a, in which case it remains as it is. These direct relative particles are: owa-aba-;

1. Direct relative construction in immediate past tense.
a. positive construction.
Pattern: Type B DRP + kha + VR + a
Uno niye owakhateekha. - This is the one who has just cooked.
Note: There is no simple past and present perfect forms in the
relative construction. It is all simple past tense.
b. negative construction.
Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + kha + VR + a + ta/tawe
Ourakhtsia tawe niRita. - The one who has not just gone is .
Rita.
2. Indirect relative construction.
a. positive construction.
Pattern: IRP + Type B SP + kha + VR + a
Owa mwakhalola ngowuno. - The one whom you have just seen is
this one here.
b. negative construction.
Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + rea + kha + VR + a
Omwana owa araakhalola ta ali heena? - Where is the child whom
he has not just now seen?

CHAPTER 12
Possessive Particles
Pattern: PC + a' If the pronominal concord ends in a, no a is added.
The possessive particles do not always indicate possession. Such expressions as "a cup of tea," "a man of truth," "a person of afar," etc. use the possessive particle. The possessive particle can be prefixed to nouns, adverbs, and infinitives, thus forming adjectival expressions.
omundu wehale - a far-away person abandu bakhale - ancient people
amakhwa katoto - true words omundu weshinani - a diligent or
enandi chiabeseen - the people's persevering person
possessions
omubano okwokhukhalake - a cutting knife (knife for cutting)
When the possessive is joined to an infinitive, a locative, or noun, the Baluyia like to prefix the initial vowel.

Those have been cooked. 6.The woman has become very tired, because she has been digging the whole day. 7.I brought good drinking water just this morning. 8.All the fruit has been picked by the children. 9.Mother dug the potatoes that we might cook them. 10.The maize has been put away (in the granary). 11.The lamb blazed all night. 12.The hour has come; let us go home. 13.The bowl has been being hunted, and it has been found by the girl. 14.The firewood was gathered by that old woman. 15.Many songs were sung in the church.
4. Polysyllabic verbs.
a. Verbs having a long ultimate vowel in the root:
Pattern: VR + ile/ilenje (active)
handiik- + ila = handiichile. Ahandiichile ibarwa. - He wrote a letter.
Pattern: VR + ilwe/ilungwe (passive)
handiichilwe. Ibarwa vihandiichilwe. - The letter was written.
b. Verbs having a short ultimate vowel in the root:
Pattern: VR with ultimate vowel doubled + e/enje (active)
khalal- = khalak + e = khalasche. Akhalache omuksaate. - She cut the bread.
Pattern: VR with ultimate vowel doubled + we/ungwe (passive)
Omukaate kukhalazkwe. - The bread has been cut.
The tone-patterns for polysyllabic verbs vary greatly. Derived forms have a relationship to the basic verb roots. Other verbs seem irregular, but this is probably because they are some type of derived form. The following table gives some of the regular tone-patterns. The vowel-stem verbs seem more regular than the consonant-stem verbs.

Have/Has Been How Long?
For expressing "how many hours/days/weeks/months/years" a person has
been doing something, one uses the immediate past or near past tense.
For expressing "how long?" these tenses are used together with the
words okuhuela, eshise, and oluaaboo/oluhoono. Helo = be enough/equal;
eshise (inyanga) = period of time; oluhoono/oluaaboo = long period of
time.
Exercise 39
Kalukhasia mulusuungu:
1.Kefa wakhayinzila Nairobi emiyika chitaru. 2.Khubeele ekima emiyika
chime. 3.Abando yabo baknalima omukunda kwabwe amachuma kabili, ne
beshili okhakale. 4.Omukhaana wakhamba musibitali tsinyanga tsiraano,
ne ashili butawa cmalwale. 5.Abeelee ewabo lichuuma elala. 6.Kabolee
abelee omukholi waChanye emiyika chiraano. 7.Mwakhaba mwAfrika emiyika
chinge? Khwakhaba mwAfrika emiyika chiraano. 8.Obeelee omwilwatsi
(omukambi) emiyika chinga? Embelee omwilwatsi (omukambi) emiyika
likumi namunaane. 9.Wakhaba hano okuhela eshise (or, oluhoono/oluaaboo)
shina? 10.Abeelee Nairobi eshise (or, oluhoono/oluaaboo) shina?
Abeeleyo eshise eshirambi (or, oluhoono/oluaaboo).
Exercise 40
Kalukhasia mululuyia:
1.Kefa has worked three years in Nairobi. 2.We have been at Kima
four years. 3.Those people have dug their garden two weeks, and they
are not yet finished. 4.The girl has spent five days in hospital,
she is still just a sick person. 5.She has been at her father's home
one week. 6.Kabolee has been John's workman five years. 7.How many
years have you been in Africa? We have been in Africa five years.
8.How many years have you been a preacher? I have been a preacher
for eighteen years. 9.How long have you been here? 10.How long has
he been at Nairobi. He has been there a long time.
Telling Time
Luyia uses the same system as Swahili in reckoning time. The new day
begins at seven o'clock in the evening (issa ndale - hour one), and
goes through the night until seven o'clock the next evening. A twentyfour
hour day is divided into two periods of twelve hours each,
from seven o'clock in the evening to seven in the morning is the
first part called eshilo/obutukhu = night. The second part, eshiteere
/omubasu = daytime, is from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. The entire twentyfour
hour day is called inyanga/litukhu. Thus there is a difference
of 6 hours in the Luyia and English systems of reckoning time:
isa ndala
7 a.m. or 7 p.m.
tsisea tsibilili
8 a.m. or 8 p.m.
tsisea tsitaru
9 a.m. or 9 p.m.
tsisea tsine
10 a.m. or 10 p.m.
tsisea tsirano
11 a.m. or 11 p.m.
tsisea tsisassaba (tsieshilo/
tsiotbutukhu)
12 midnight
tsisea tsisassaba (tsieshteere/
tsiomubasu)
12 noon
tsisea musafu
1 a.m. or 1 p.m.
tsisea munaane
2 a.m. or 2 p.m.
tsisea shienda
3 a.m. or 3 p.m.
tsisea likumi
4 a.m. or 4 p.m.
tsisea likumi nandala
5 a.m. or 5 p.m.
tsisea likumi natsibilii
6 a.m. or 6 p.m.
Many people use the Swahili terms for telling time and nearly everyone
uses the Swahili for 12, 1, and 3 o'clock: saa sita = 12 o'clock;
saa saba = 1 o'clock; and saa tisa = 3 o'clock. The difference between
a.m. and p.m., when necessary, is indicated by adding tsieshilo
/tsiotbutukhu = of the night; tsionukamba = of the morning; tsiokhubwile
= of the afternoon; tsionukolooba = of the evening; "Dawn"
is mumabwibi. Early morning is mukamba tsuli. All night is eshile
shiosi/obutukhu bwosi. All day is inyanga yosi/litukhu lioo. For
7 a.m. or p.m. the possessive particle ya- is used instead of tsia-

The half-hours are indicated by giving the hour and adding neinusu = and a half. A minute is itakika; to express minutes after the hour, we say netsitakika + the number of minutes. To express minutes before the hour we say netsitakika + number of minutes followed by okhuula isaa/taisaas + the hour - it is minutes ____ to arrive at hour(s) _____. Thus:
Netsisa tsine neinusu. It is 10:30 (lit. It is hours four and a half,)
Neisa ndala netsitakika likhum. It is 7:10
Netsitakika likhum natsireano okhuula tsisa munaane.
Netsisa tsinga?
What time is it (lit. It is hours how many)?

Netsisa tsinga? Netsisaas munaane netsitakika likhum natsiraano. 3.
Tsisa tsizasabi (sa a sita) tsuille. Teisikaale tsitakika amakhumi kabili natsibili. 4.Tsisa mussafu (sa a saba) tsuille. Ee, ne tsibirilemo
tsitakika tsiraano. 5.Tsisa shienda (sa a tisa) tsuille, noho? Ee, tsakhoola. Netsisaas shienda (nisa tisa) habwene (or, mumondi). 6.Wenya enzite liima? Witse mukamba mukolooba isaa ndala.
7.Netsisa tsinga? Netsisa tsibili nende inusu tsiomukamba. 8.Khwenya
khutse liina? Khwenya okhutse leelo, tsisa tsine. 9.Omutoka kurulanga hano tsisa shime. Kurulanga hano buli nyanga tsisa likhum
. 10.Asa aliho? Tawe, atsili Kakamega mukamba kuno. O! atsili
tsisa tsinga? Tsisa tsitaru. 11.Abacheni beetsile? Ee, beetsile tsisa likhum nandala. 12.Paps akaluwushe okhurula Nairobi tsisa tsiraano neinusu eshilo shino/outbukhu bunu. (When speaking of last night or the coming night, the Baluyu say "this night" - eshilo shino or outbukhu bunu. If it is the past night, the past tense of the verb is used. If it is the coming night, the near future tense is used.) 13.Netsisa tsinga? Netsitakika amakhumi kabili natsiraano okhuula tsisa mussafu (saba). 14.Netsisa tsinga okhurula tsisa munaane okhuula tsisa likhum? Nitsibili.

When do you want me to come? Come tomorrow evening at seven o'clock. 7.What time is it? It is eight-thirty in the morning. 8.When do we need to go? We need to go today at ten o'clock. 9.At what time does the car leave here? It leaves here every day at four o'clock. 10.Is Arthur here? No, he went to Kakamega this morning. Oh! what time did he go? Nine o'clock. 11.Have the guests come? Yes, they came at five o'clock. 12.Father returned from Nairobi at eleven-thirty last night. 13.What time is it? It is twenty-five minutes to one. 14.How many hours are there from two to four? There are two.

CHAPTER 13
Relative Construction
Both the direct and indirect relative particles are formed from the
pronominal concords. The direct relative particles fall into two
groups, Type A and Type B. Type A is used with present tense, near
past, three future tenses which will be studied later, and with all
negative relative construction.
1. Direct relative particle.
Pattern: IV + PC (Type A)
Pattern: IV + PC + a (Type B)
These are the subject prefixes of the relative clause and are always
prefixed to the relative clause verb.
2. Indirect relative particle.
Pattern: IV + PC + a
These do not vary and are always written separately. Their uses
are (a) object of the relative clause, (b) for expressing "whom"
or "which" one has, and (c) for expressing the possessive pronoun
"whose," in which case the possessive particle is always used also.
In relative negative construction the subject prefixes, whether
relative particles or the ordinary ones, are always Type A. If the
tense is one which ordinarily takes the Type B prefixes, the extra
a is added to the ra negative, thus: raa.
Table of Relative Particles

These expressions are all formed from the ni copula from which the
i has been elided, leaving only the n. The usual rules of nasalization

Pattern: n(i) + PC + IV + Demonstrative (for all others) near)

begin with vowels are used, ss, oyo, abo, okwo, etc.

If any verb follows any of the above forms, it must be in relative construction. These forms are used when the object spoken of can be seen and pointed out (with the chin!). It will have been noted that the w vowel glide is used before those demonstratives which begin with u.
