"Once, twice, three times (three-fold), four times (four-fold), etc., are formed using ordinal numbers: lulala - once, or, khandi lulala; khabili, or, khandi khabili - twice, two-fold; khataru, or, khandi khataru - three times, three-fold;khandi khane; khandi khersano; khandi khasasasa; khandi musafu; khandi munaane; khandi shienda; khandi ekhumi/likhumi; khandi likhumi nalulala; khandi likhumi na- khabili; etc.

Exercise 30
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.Do you see this cat? Yes, I see it. 2.Have you just chopped off the banana leaves? Yes, I have just chopped them off. 3.How do you count the days of one week? I count them like this: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven. 4.Where is the saucepan? Anzemo is washing it outside. 5.The father wants to buy shoes for his boy. Where can he get them? 6.This book is good. Do you want to read it? 7.Pick the flowers now. I am picking them. 8.Is the owner of the banana patch chopping off leaves in it today? Yes, he is chopping them off in it. 9.Fry the meat. I just now fried it. 10.Tell Sarah to set the table. Oh! she has just finished setting it. 11.Arthur, herd the cow. I am herding it. 12.Sing (pl.) this song. We have just sung it. 13.Grandmother is telling stories. Do you hear them? Yes, I hear them. 14. Are you doing arithmetic now? Yes, I am doing it now. 15.Is the sheep nursing the lamb? Yes, it is nursing it. 16.Sweep the tiny rooms. I am sweeping them. 17.Do you see the face of that goat? Yes, I see it. 18.Look how that giant yonder is carrying the huge club! My goodness! He is carrying it on his head.
Near Past Tense of Verbs
This tense is used for anything which has happened today only. For this time span there is the simple past and the present perfect tense. With the exception of the subject prefix for the 3rd person singular the difference is a matter of tone. The subject prefix for the 3rd person singular in the present perfect tense is u before consonants and w before vowels. Otherwise all subject prefixes for this tense are type A, the same as for the present tense.
1.Monosyllabic verbs. Active.

fw + ile = zwile - died, has/have died
Passive
Group a: Pattern:VS + ilwe/ilunge (long coalescence)
ha + ilwe = heelwe - was/were given,has/have been given
Group b: Pattern:VR + ilwe/ilunge
ri + ilwe = rilwe - was/were feared,has/have been feared

With the exception of the 3rd person singular there is no way in
writing to show the difference between the simple past and the present
perfect tense in the Near Past time span. The real difference is
one of tone. There is a range of five tones for verbs in this tense;
high, medium-high, medium, medium-low, and low. For representing
these tones the following chart can be a guide:

A dash represents the medium tone:
A dot one space above represents a medium-high tone:
A dot two spaces above represents a high tone:
A dot one space below represents a medium-low tone:
A dot two spaces below represents a low tone:

In the simple present stem of the monosyllabic verbs there are four
which are spoken on a lower tone than the others. These four follow
a different tone-pattern than the others in the simple past, but all
follow the same tone-pattern in the present perfect tense form. The
following tone-patterns with the verbs in their proper classifications
are shown in the chart given below.

Tone-Patterns for Monosyllabic Verbs in the Near Past
| Infinitive | Simple Past | Present Perfect |
|------------|-------------|----------------|
| okhushia   | bushieele   | bushieele       |
| okhube     | abeelee     | ubeelee         |
| okhura     | areelee     | ureelee         |
| okhua      | aheelee     | uheelee         |

Note that all present perfect tense tones are on a lower tone-pattern

The simple past translated into English is of course: I ate, you ate, he/she ate, we ate, you ate, they ate, it ate, they ate, etc. The present perfect form is: I have eaten, you have eaten, he/she has eaten, we have eaten, you have eaten, they have eaten, it has eaten. All verbs do not fit completely into these two forms exactly as they do in English. But this true of all languages; no one form is the exact equivalent in every way to any other one form in another language.

Exercise 31
Kalukhasis muLusungu:
1.Abacheni babeelohelo leelo. 2.Amatsti kali heena? Kabeeloh hamo mu-kamba kuno. 3.Nyina uheele omwana amatsi anywe. 4.Amatsti kahweele. 5.Mbeela abasaana omukate. 0! kwosi kuhweele. 6.Oreels heema omubano? Engureele hano. 7.Abakhanaa basie amatuuma bulsano. Basieele mukamba kuno. 8.Kukhu afwile mushilo (mubutukhu), ne bulsano omulwale uno yeenya okhufwa. 9.Amakanda kailiwe nende abasaana kosi pe. 10.Ebikombe bireelwe mukabsti. 11.Tsing'ombe tsitsile heena? Tsitsile okhwaya. 12.Amatsti kayiile. 13.Amatsti kayiile bulayi mukamba kuno. 14.Bushieele. 15.Bushieele bwangu mukamba kuno. 16.Umanyie abakholi nibatsille.

Exercise 32
Kalukhasis muLuluyisa:
1.The guests were here today. 2.Where is the water? It was here this morning. 3.The mother has given the child some water to drink (that he may drink). 4.The water is gone (has come to an end). 5.Give the child some bread for me. Oh, it is all gone (it has all come to an end). 6.Where did you put the knife? I put it here. 7.The girls may grind the maize now. They ground it this morning. 8.Grandmother died in the night, and now this sick person is about to die. 9.The beans have all been eaten by the children. 10.The cups have been put in the cupboard. 11.Where have the cows gone? They have gone to graze. 12.The water is hot (has become hot). 13.The water got hot well this morning. 14.Good morning (it has become light). 15.It got light quickly this morning. 16.Let me know when the workmen have gone.

2. Verbs ending in -ia.
Active.
Pattern:VR + ye/yenje
kasi + ye = kasiye. Engasiye ingubo. - I fixed the dress.
osi + yenje = osiyenje. Yoosiyenje ebikombe. - She has been washing the cups.

Passive.
Pattern: VR + ibwe/ibungwe
kusi + ibwe = kusibwe. Amakanda kakusibwe. - The beans were sold.
kosi + ibungwe = kosiibungwe. Amapesa kakosiibungwe. - The money has been being lost.

In the simple past the polysyllabic verbs ending in -ia seem to follow one general pattern of tone: medium, high, medium, low. The tone patterns of the dissyllabic verbs vary according to the pitch in the present tense stem. A table of some of the verbs and their tone patterns for infinitives and past tenses follow.

Absolute Pronouns
We have used the absolute pronouns for the person class very much. Their formation is irregular. But all other absolute pronouns follow a regular pattern of formation.
Pattern: PC + o
Ku + o = kwo; ku + o = kwo, etc.
All pronominal concords ending in a coalesce short with the o.
ba + o = bo; ka + o = ko; kha + o = kho; ha + o = ho.
Besides being used alone to express contrast or clarity of though, there are six combinations of absolute pronouns. We shall study five of these combinations in this chapter, and the sixth, which is the use of the possessive particle with absolute pronouns to form possessive adjectives and possessive pronouns, will be studied in the next chapter. The following tables show the absolute pronouns for all classes with five combinations.

Relative Construction in the Intermediate Past Tense
1.Consonant stems, direct relative.
Positive. Pattern: Type B DRP + VR + same endings as near past
Negative. Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + VR + same endings as near past tense
2.Vowel stems, direct relative.
Positive. Pattern: Type B DRP + ya + VR + near past endings
Negative. Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + ya + VR + near past endings
3.Consonant stems, indirect relative.
Positive. Pattern: IRP + Type B SP + VR + near past endings
Negative. Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + raa + VR + near past endings
4.Vowel stems, indirect relative.
Positive. Pattern: IRP + Type B SP + ya + VR + near past endings
Negative. Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + raa + ya + VR + near past endings

shorts) were many. 7.The tobacco which was smoked by the people was
very strong. 8.The lamps which were lit burned well. 9.The belt
which the boy put on is long, and the one which he did not put on is
short. 10.The tiny story which was not heard by these children is one
of children of long ago. 11.The tiny chickens which the girl didn't
feed are hungry. 12.There is the little cupboard in which the cups
were put. 13.The thirst which the man felt when he was tired was
fierce. 14.The cabinetmaking which the cabinet maker didn't finish
yesterday is going to be finished today. 15.The fireplace where people
sat yesterday was fixed today.
There are no separate forms or different tones in relative construction
to differentiate between the simple past and the present perfect
tenses.

Possessive Adjectives and Pronouns
See pages 30 and 57 for a revision of possessive adjectives and pronouns
. They are a combination of initial vowels, possessive particles,
and absolute pronouns,
1.Possessive adjectives.
a.second and third persons singular, always short coalescence.
(1) shortened suffix form.
Pattern: PP + u (2nd person) -woi:-boi:-kwoi:-chio, etc.
Pattern: PP + e (3rd person) -wei:-kwe:-chie:-be, etc.
(2) long form; stands alone.
Pattern: PC + PP + o ( kukwo;chichio, etc.
Exception: The person class prefixes a w- before PC + wuwo.
Pattern: PC + PP + e (3rd person) uuwe;kukwe;chichie.
pronominal concords ending in a:
Pattern: PP + o/e + PP + o/e babo,bebe;koko,keke, etc.
Some dialects hold to the patterns under (2) above, as,
baboo;kakoo;khakho hahoo;babe;kake;khakhe;hahe.
b.all other persons and classes.
Pattern: PP + AP
Table for Forming Possessive Adjectives and Possessive Pronouns
The pronominal concords are given in parentheses for use with
the 2nd and 3rd persons singular of the person class when forming
the long forms: kukwo;chichie;okukwo;echichie, etc.

For Past Tense of Verbs
1.Consonant stem verbs. (from fifth day on back indefinitely)
Simple past and present perfect tenses:
Pattern: Type B SF + VR + a
Ndatsia. - I went. Batsia. - They have gone.
The tone for the simple past is relatively low on the subject prefix. The tone for the present perfect is high on the subject prefix. This is true for both consonant and vowel stem verbs.
2.Vowel stem verbs.
a.simple past:
Pattern: Type B SF + VR + a (long coalescence)
Khweetsa. - We came. Beeka bulayi. - They studied well.
b.present perfect:
Pattern: Type B SF + ya + VR + a (long coalescence)
Khwayeska butinyu. - We have studied hard.
Object prefix "me" for immediate past and far past present perfect tense is yan.
Conjugations
Simple Past (Consonant) Present Perfect
Singular Plural Singular Plural
ndatsia khwatsia ndatsia khwatsia
watsia mwatsia watsia mwatsia
yatsia batsia yatsia batsia
(vowel)
ndeebaala khweebaala ndyeebaala khweebaala
weebaala mweebaala weyeebaala mweebaala
yeebaala beebaala wayeebaala bayeebaala
The continuous endings are the same as for those for the various types of verbs in the present tense. However, the meaning is usually "used to do." The far past continuous ending for the verb "to be" is -nji. Yalini omwechesia. - He used to be a teacher. To indicate that a thing was in the process of being done, a compound form is used. This will be studied later.
Simple Far Past with Consonant Stems

Remember that in actual writing the diacritical marks in these exercises are not used. These are merely to indicate the high tone for the student. Some dialects have only y- instead of the ye- prefixed to vowel stem verbs. This will be noted in the various pronunciation
Relative Construction in the Far Past Tense
There seem to be no differences of tone or form to differentiate between the simple past and the present perfect tenses within this far past time span.in relative construction.
1.Consonant stems (or with a following prefix which begins with a consonant).
Positive construction (direct relative):
Pattern: Type B DRP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga
Omundu owatsia ngwuwuno. - Here is the person who went.
Negative construction:
Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga + ta/tawe
Ouraatsia ta, ngwooyo. - There is the one who did not go.
(indirect relative)
Positive construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type B SP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga
Omwana, owa omukhaana valola, ailanga. - The child whom the girl saw is crying.
Negative construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type A SP + raa + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga + ta/tawe
Omwana, owa omukhaana arealola ta,bulaand ngwowulia. - The child whom the girl did not see is now over yonder.
2.Vowel stems.
Positive construction. (direct relative):
Pattern: Type B DRP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga (long coalescence)
Omusaala okwaama ebiamo ebinji ngwokuno. - The tree which has borne much fruit is this one.
Negative construction:
Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + ya + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga + ta
Omusaala okuraasyama ebiamo ebinji ta ngwokwo. - There is the tree which did not bear much fruit.
(indirect relative)
Positive construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type B SP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga
Abeechi, aba omwechesia veechesia, nabachesi. - The pupils whom the teacher taught are clever.
Negative construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type A SP + raa + ya + VR + a + ta
Abaana, aba khurasyosia ta, bali abamali. - The children whom we did not wash were dirty.

(are) those of hunger. 11.These are the nuts which will sell for (be
exchanged for) a deer price. 12.This is the boat which the man will
finish building next month, and that one is the one which he will
not finish at that time. 13.The quailbasket, which that weaver yonder
is weaving, is the one which will be finished in the next four days.
14.These are the eggs which will be hatched in the next ten days.
Emphasis
There many means for adding emphasis to Luyia expressions.
1.Pattern: PC + ene (as an adverbial superlative expression)
Omutoka nomulayi kwene. - The car is simply grand.
2.By using okhushila, muno, okhushila muno, or munonono.
Akholanga bulayi okhushila. - He is doing exceedingly well.
Orio munonono! - Thank you very, very much.

3.By using interjections. (to be studied more fully later)

4.By using absolute pronouns.
Iwe shiukhoonyile tawe. - You did not help me.
Shiyakhoonyile isie ta. - She did not help me.
5.An infinitive of the main verb at the beginning of a sentence intensifies the verb.
Okhukhoonya shiukhoonyile ta. - You did not help me.
6.By using a double object.
Emulutsi omundu uyo. - I have seen that man.
7.By using ni copula with absolute pronouns.
Uno niye ouyinzilanga butinyu. - This is the one who is working hard.
8.By changing the word order in a sentence.
Tsing'ombe yitsio, omwayi atsiayang'a. - Those cows, the shephe is herding them.
9.By using nahatuutu ta or kata nahatuutu ta in a negative statement
Omukhaena shiyakhoonyile omushiele kata nahatuutu ta. - The girl did not help the old woman at all.
Shibamuchamile hatuutu ta. - They did not like him at all.
10.By using -kho in a negative statement to intensify it. This has been used often in this book.
Shiamilekho leelo ta. - She did not dig at all today.
11.By repeating verb stem, to which bu- has been prefixed, immediately following the main verb. It has the idea of going right on with a thing.

12.By using ideophones. (to be studied more fully later)
O! neshiilima ti. - Oh! it is pitch dark.
Akorile koro. - He was completely lost.
13.By repeating a noun with na- in place of the initial vowel to express the idea of "a mere," or "an ordinary...," etc.
Omwana namwana anyala okhukola yako. - A mere child can do th

Augmentative Verbs
This derived form is formed in the same way as the Reversive. But
the meanings of these verbs are an augmentation of the meaning of
the original verb. The meanings of the various forms will make it
clear to the student whether the verbs are reversive or augmentative.
All verbs do not appear in all forms. In fact, no one verb appears in
all the derived forms. If a verb is in the reversive, it cannot
be in the augmentative, and vice versa.
1.Verbs whose ultimate vowel of the root is a, e, i, or u.
Pattern:VR + ula/ulula/ula
ching + ula = chinguala - raise, lift up.
In the ula suffix the first l of the ulula seems to have dropped
out leaving ula.
2.Verbs whose ultimate vowel of the root is o.
Pattern: VR + ola/ola/ola
lond + oola = londoola - follow along a path or trail.
Again it seems that the ola is the ola ending with the first l
elided.

Relative Construction in the "Li" Future
1.Direct relative.
Positive.
Pattern: Type A DRP + li + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga
Oullitsia niwing? - Who is it who will go?
Negative.
Pattern: Type A DRP + ra + li + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga + ta/taw
Abaralitsia ta - They who will not go.
2.Indirect relative.
Positive.
Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + li + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga
Omundu, owa alilola - The person whom he will see.
Negative.
Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + ra + li + VR + a/anga, etc. + ta/taw
Gmutoka,okwa aralilola ta - The car which he will not see.

Ideophones
Ideophones are a separate part of speech in Luyia. Their function is similar to that of an adverb. They seek to imitate the sound of the idea which a word represents. They add meaning to verbs, adjectives, nouns, etc. They may be monosyllabic, disyllabic, or polysyllabic, and have definite tone patterns. Many are used only with specific words. The first two in the list below can be used with many kinds of words, while the others are more limited.
Matching words Ideophones Sentences
many used po - much, very Nobubbi po. - It is very bad.
many used pe - all Amokonda Rahucole pe. - The beans are all gone.

Extensive Verbs
These verbs indicate an extended or repeated action, at times. At other times they are used in a polite sense, as, "please do so-and-so." Again, depending on the tone of voice, they may be used to express exasperation: Well, go ahead and do it then.
Mbeelaka. - Please excuse me; or, Mbeelaka. - Well, just go ahead and put up with me!
Voice intonation makes the difference.
1.Monsyllabic verbs.
Pattern: VS + itsaka (coalescing group a)
Nyweetsaka. - Please drink.
Pattern: VR + itsaka (non-coalescing group b)
Liitsaka. - Please go ahead and eat.
2.Verbs (not monosyllabic) ending in -ia.
Pattern: VR + chie
Kasichie ingubu. - Please fix the dress.
3.All other verbs.
Pattern: VS + ka
4.When verb stems end in -e, as subjunctive mood or imperative plural
a.monsyllabic use itseche
b.other verbs ending in -ia follow Pattern: VR + chie
c.all other verbs follow Pattern: VR + e + che

nala (ng'aya) - become accustomed/ adjusted to, be usual/customary
shinda,cheleva (cheleba) - be late, tarry
laama - bequeath, beseech, pray
obulaame - inheritance
omukhalachi - judge
omusikari - policeman,soldier
omweha - bride
isindu - quail
tsilila - get wet
yabila - bury
chelela - return (home)
Evana - term of respect to a man; abaakukas - ancestors, grand-fathers
eshilindwa - grave
eshilifu - chest
ebweneyo - right there.
Conditional Clause "If"
The ni construction which we studied in Chapter 6 could be interpreted as "if," "when," or "and." There is a reduplicated form of ni construction which means only "if."
Pattern: ni + SP + ba + ni + SP + VS (positive)
Pattern: ni + SP + ba + ni + SP + ra + VS + ta (negative)
Conjugations
tsia
Singular
1st per. nimba ninzia - if I go
2nd per. noba notsia - if you go
3rd per. naba natsia - if he/she goes
Plural
nikhuba nikutsia - if we go
nimuba nimutsia - if you go
nibabs nibatsitsanga - if they are going (new or always)
nikuba nikutsia - if it goes etc.
tsia
1st per. nimba ninzitsa - if I come nikhuba nikritsa - if we come
2nd per. noba niwitsa - if you come nimuba nimitsa - if you come
3rd per. naba nyeetsa - if he/she nibaba nibetsa - if they come etc.
The second form in this "if" clause can be in the present tense as given above: nibaba nibatsia - if they go.
Or it may be in a past tense: nibaba nibatsiile - if they have gone.
Or it may be in a future tense:nibaba nibatsie - if they shall go.
The main clause may express many things: commands, both imperative and subjunctive; clauses using enya, nyala, etc. followed by infinitives or subjunctive forms; wishes, instructions, desires, permissions, etc. in the subjunctive mood; or a statement in a future tense.
Exercise 1
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Noba nomulola, mubolele yeetsa. 2.Nimube nimutsia Nairobi, munderele ingubo imbia. 3.Nimba ninyoole eshitabo yishio, enyenya okhushisoome. 4.Nibaba naekhole bulayi mumareebu, nababire mumukanda kwakhataru. 5.Omutoka nikuba nakukasibwe mukamba, khwakhatsie Nakuru teinyanga taine nitsihwele. 6.Noba niwenya, onyala okhunaba bulayi. 7.Tsing'ombe tsino-tsibili nitsiba hitsikhomele, khulitsisiza mu-shiselelo. 8.Omwayi naba narayanga tsimbusi bulayi, shitsilikhomela bulayi tawe. 9.Nimba nimulola, nemubolele okhvitse okhukhaaonya. 10.Petero naba nalio, yeembe olwimbo bulaso. 11.Ifule niyiba niyitsa lichuuma lino, nakhura sche omukunda. 12.Ebiano nibibe nibienjile, khwakhabinochche Okwakhabili.

4.If they succeed (do well) in the examinations, they will pass into the third class. 5.If the car will be fixed tomorrow, we shall go to Nakuru four days hence. 6.If you (s.) want to, you are able to sew well. 7.If these two cows are fat, we shall kill them for the wedding (during the wedding). 8.If the shepherd does not herd the goats well, they will not fatten well. 9.If I see her, I will tell her to come to visit you (s.). 10.If Peter is here, he may sing now. 11.If the rain comes this week, we shall plant the garden. 12.If the fruit is ripe (has ripened), we shall pick it Tuesday.
Contingent Mood
1.The Possible Contingent.
This mood uses the "if" clause as has been studied above, while the main, or contingent, clause verb is in the immediate past tense, and represents the idea of "would," "could," and, with haundi it is interpreted as "might." It is practically the equivalent of the English past subjunctive mood, expressing the possibility of a thing happening in the future: If he came, I would tell him, etc.
Pattern: If clause + Type B SP + kha + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga
Naba nateekha, ndakhalia. - If she cooked, I would eat.
Notice that the "if" clause does not change in tense as it does for this type of sentence in English. Actually, the Muluyia says, "If she cooks, I would eat." But this is not idiomatic English to interpret it so.
The main clause uses the shi....tawe negative.
For expressing "might, might possibly:"
Pattern: If clause + haundi + Type B SP + kha + VR + a/anga,etc.
Haundi bakhatsia Nairobi. - They might possibly go to Nairobi
a.Expressing possibility:
Exercise 3
Kalukhasia muLusunga:
1.Bwana natsie Eshisumu mukamba? Haundi yakhatsis. 2.Abacheni na-beetse leelo? Haundi bakheetss. 3.Ing'ombe nayisi-nzwe leelo? Fwaha (haundi) yakhasinzwa. 4.Namuchielele ingo leelo? Haundi khwakhachelela (or in the indicative mood, Haundi nakhuche-lele - Perhaps we shall return). 5.Olanaba ingubo bulaano? Haundi ndakhanaaba. 6.Eshilindwa nashiyabwe leelo, noho? Haundi shiakha-yawa bulaano, shichila leelo abandu beenya okhuyabile oufwile.
Exercise 4
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.Will Bwana go to Kisumu tomorrow? He might possibly go. 2.Will the guests come today? They might come. 3.Will the cow be slaughtered today? Perhaps it might be slaughtered. 4.Will you return home today? We might return. 5.Will you sew the dress now? I might possibly sew (it). 6.Will the grave be dug today? It might be dug now, because today the people want to bury the dead person.
b."If" clauses with the contingent clauses:
There are some variations which are often used in the "if" clause in the contingent mood. Here are some.
Nimba ninzia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I went now, I would see him.
Nimba nindakhatsia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I should go now, I would see him.
Ninzia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I went now, I would see him.
Ndakhatsia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I should go now, I would see him.
Noba noratsia mukamba, shiwakhanyoola amakenda ta. - If you did not go tomorrow, you would not get the beans.
Noba norakhatsia mukamba, shiwakhanyoola amakenda ta. - If you should not go tomorrow, you would not get the beans.

17.About to, Seem on the Verge of.
There are two ways to say the ordinary form.
a.Pattern: SP+"tobe4ahambi + infinitive
Ali/abeele/yabeele/yali ahambi okhutsia. - He is/was about to
go.
Alaba/nabe/yakhabe/aliba ahambi okhutsia. - He will be about
to go.
b.withjenya.
(1)present tense:
Pattern: Type A SP + enya + infinitive
Omwana yeenya okhukwa. - The child seems on the verge of
falling.
(2)past tenses:
Pattern: SP + "to be",in past tense + ni + Type A SP + enya +
infinite
Yakhaba/abeele/yabeele/yali niyeenya okhutsia. - He was just
on the verge of going/about to go.
(3)future tenses:
Pattern: SP + "to be" in future tense + ni + Type A SP + enya
+ infinitive
Alaba/nabe/yakhabe/aliba niyeenya okhutsia. - He will be about
to go/just on the verge of going
Exercise 31
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Olwa khulileyo, abandu babeelie ahambi okhutsia. 2.Olwa omusakanula
yeetsa yino, yali ahambi okhukwe khulwe okhuchonge. 3.Olwa abakana
bamalile okhulima, abandu babeelie ahambi okhuchake. 4.Olwa khubeele
nikhwenya okhutsia okhukona, omundu yeetsile. 5.Olwa abanna babeele
nibeenya okhuchaka okhubaya, abanyina babalanjile. 6.Olwa omulilo
kwali shambi (kwali nikwenya) okhusima, omukhaana yarakhwo tsikwi
tsindi. 7.Nikhulileyo nakhunyooole mbu nababe ahambi okhulia. (or, nababe
nibeenya okhulia). 8.Ebitabu bino nibimalile okhwechelwamo nabeechi
, bishkabe nibili ahambi okhukofula. 9.Omwezi okwitwa nikuchaka
, amatsi keshitano shiserve kaliba nikali ahambi okhuhwa.
Exercise 32
Kalukhasia muLaluya:
1.When we arrived there, the people were about to go. 2.When the old
man came here, he was about to fall because of tiredness. 3.When the
girls finished digging, the others were about to begin. 4.When we
were just on the verge of going to bed (to sleep), the man came. 5.
When the children were just ready to begin playing, their mothers
called them. 6.When the fire was about to go out, the girl put more
firewood on it. 7.When we arrive there we shall find that they will
be about to eat. 8.After these books have been studied (in) by the
pupils, they will be nearly worn out. 9.At the beginning of next
month the water of our spring will nearly be gone.
c.Another form of "about to" is used if something happens to prevent
one from doing what he was about to do.
Pattern: SP + VS of "to be" in past or future tense + Type A SP +
subjunctive VS
Khubeele khulie olwa bakhulanjile okhutsia ninabo. - We were
just about to eat when they called us to go with them.
Nyinamwana yabeele atsie Mombasa, ne omwanawe yalwallile. - The
mother was just about to go to Mombasa, but her child became ill.
Shikhunya la okhulima bulaano ta.Nakhube khuchache, ne mama nakullanje
okhulia. - We cannot dig now. We shall be just about to
begin, and mother will call us to eat.

CHAPTER 21
Vocabulary
fuba - spoil (by not going on to completion, as food spoiled in
cooking because the fire has gone out)
longa - make; fashion or mold with the hands
-shiamu - crooked
omukhulundu - elder, mature person, adult
Denominative Verbs
These are verbs which are derived from substantive nouns, adjectives,
and adverbs. With only an occasional exception, they are formed by
adding -kha,-ha,-ia, or -hala to the noun or adjective stem, or to
adverb. The overall idea is "to become" a certain way.
1.Those formed with -kha.
Word Stem
-lunjji - straight,righteous
kololi - straight forward, up-
-lamu - well,healthy,alive
eshimuli - flower,blossom
-lalu - mad, insane
Derived Form
lunjikha - straighten up/out,become
straight
kololokha - become straight/correct
/right
lamukha - revive,come to life
mulikha - bloom,blossom
lalukha - go mad/insane
2.Those formed with -ha.
-ochi - sharp
-imbichiti - short
-cheni - strange,new, visitor
-khongo - great, important,big
-chesi - wise,intelligent,clever
Derived Form
ochiha - become sharp
imbiha - shrink,become shorter
cheniha - visit,stay while
khongoha - become great,big,etc.
chesiha (chetsiha) - become wise/
clever
-tiiti - small, little
-inji - much, many
-rambi - tall, long
-kali - large, big, great
-khungu - old
-omwami - chief, chief person
Derived Form
tiitha - become small/little
injhe - multiply,become many
rambiha - become tall/long
kaliha - become large/big/great
khunguha - become old (people)
amilha - hold ruling position,reign
3.Those formed with -la.
-tofu - weak,lazy,lacking in determination
-bofu - blind
-kofu - old,mature,worn out
kuukhu - grandmother
Derived Form
tofula - become weak/lazy/lacking
in determination
bofula - become/go blind
kofula - become old/mature/worn
kuukhula - become/act slow like
an old woman
4.Those formed from -hala.
omukumba - a barren woman
-chesi - wise,clever,intelligent
-kara - lazy
omuyinda - rich/wealthy person
-nyelele - narrow,slender,fine
Derived Form
kumbahala - become barren
chesihala - become wise/clever
karahala - become lazy
yindihala - become rich/wealthy
nyelehala - become slender/thin;
shrink as a withered arm/leg
Many of these derived verbs can be put in the causative and other
forms: lunjisia - straighten; lamusia - revive,bring to life; injivia
- multiply (tr.), cause to increase.

Exercise 4
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.That boy barely got his hands wet washing them this morning. 2.The
children hopped about for joy. 3.That person yonder marries one woman,
lives with her awhile, then sends her away and marries another one, over and over. 4.That boy reads every book he can get. 5.
I only glanced at the letter; I did not read it thoroughly. 6.A woman
gets up and lies down again and again when she is in labour. 7.Cain
was made to leave his country, and he went and wandered about in the
whole earth. 8.Where are you going? I am just taking a walk. 9.This
child is naughty; he hacks up everything he sees. 10.This tree blooms
profusely every year.
Summary of "And"
1. nina- is used for "and" before an absolute pronoun in multiple
subjects and objects in a sentence.
iwe ninaye muli abasaana butswa. - You and he are only children.
Endutsi inywe ninabo bosi. - I saw you and them also.
Omusiani ninabo batsiltsanga ingo. - The boy and they are going
home.
2. a.na- joins nouns, and all but the last in a series of nouns.
omwanu nomukheana nomukhasi nende omussatsa. - a child and a girl
and a woman and a man.
b.As a conjunctive between clauses, denoting change of subject.
Abakhana bakhoonyanga omushiele, naye alimanga. - The girls are
helping the old woman, and she is digging.
Iwe olitiitsanga, nasi endeekhanga. - You are eating and I am cookNote
that na- in this usage is with absolute pronouns.
ing.
c.As a conjunctive between infinitives indicating a sequence of acts.
Omukhasi msietsanga, nokhufuka obusuma, nokhussia mamuchele,henokhulisisa
abama. - The girl grinds and makes obusuma, and goes
for water and feeds the children.
3. nende is used in joining two nouns used as multiple subjects or
objects in a sentence, also before the last noun or infinitive in a
series.
Omukhasi nende omussatsa balimanga. - The woman and man are digging
.
Omukhasi nomukheana nende omussatsa balimanga. - The woman and
girl and man are digging.
Yeenya okhufuka nende okhulia. - She wants to make obusuma and
eat.
4. khandi a.joins two or more adjectives describing the same noun or
pronoun.
Yohana nomurambi khandi nomunyelele. - John is tall and slender.
Oli omusiro khandi omwimbichiti. - You are fat and short.
b.for joining two or more adverbs describing the same verb.
Yee lukhanga bwangu khandi butinyu. - He is running fast and hard.
c.joining two or more independent clauses having no time sequence
referring to the same subject.
Omundu uno ayinzilanga bulayi, khandi ayinzilange bwangu. - This
man works well, and he works fast.
d.joining two or more independent clauses of no time sequence which
refer to two or more subjects doing the same thing, or being the
same way.
Abakhana balimanga, khandi abasiani balimenge leelo. - The girls
are digging, and the boys are digging today.
5. ni-, or consecutive construction. See page 161. This seems to be
used when a sequence of events are related.
Mana natsia niyeelukha nalanga abandu nababoolela. - Then he went
running and called the people and told them.
6. ne as a conjunctive between a dependent and independent clause,or
those having time sequence. It is also used for "but."

More Uses of "kha"
This is a form which adds verbosity to one's speech, making it more
informal, sometimes playful, sometimes taking from the bluntness of
straightforward speech.
1. Commands.
Pattern: kha + subjunctive stem (for both singular and plural)
Khatsie. - Just go along, go ahead.
2. With tenses.
Pattern: SP + kha + VS in desired tense
Kakhali karie? - What's the matter here? or, Just what is wrong?
Exercise 5
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Ekhenya okhuboola likhuwa, Khaboole. 2.Khukhatsia bulasano, noho?
Khatsie. 3.Notsie Nairobi, nokhakaluše bwangu. 4.Sing'ombe tsikhanyeеле
amatesi, nohomba tsishili? 5.Omusaala kulia kukhakhlunga
kurie? 6.Eshimeeme shielikondi shikharfwele moushina? 7.Ambeele kakhaweele
bwangu leele mbushina? 8.Okhalli namakhuwa shina? 9.Okhatekhe
shina? 10.Mukhahenganga shina?
Exercise 6
Kalukhasia muDuluyia:
1.I would just like to say a word. Go ahead and say it. 2.Shall we
just go now? Go ahead. 3.If you go to Nairobi, you will just come
straight back. 4.Now have the cows drunk water, or not yet? 5.That
tree yonder, just how is it growing? 6.Just why did the lamb die?
7.Why ever was the milk finished so quickly today? 8.Now what affares
de you (s.)-happen to have? 9.Just what are you (s.) cooking?
10.Whatever are you (pl.) looking at.
Both
There is a term which varies from one dialect to another, but which
in some means "both," or "they are included." This is the use of
ali...ali; Abana balihe, ali abasiani, ali abakhama. The children
were there, both boys and girls. Some dialects use hali...hali;
others ari...ari; and still others khali...khali.
Another way of saying "both," meaning two is:
Pattern: plural AP + mbi
bombi, chiombi, kombi, biombi, tsionambi, rwombi, etc.
Pattern: plural AP + si + plural NOP + bili
bosi babili, chiosi chibili, kosi kabilii, biosi bibili, tsiosi
tsibili, rwosi rubili, etc.
Shortened Forms and Contractions
1. Interrogatives heena? shina? wina? beena? mbushina? liina? become
: he? shi? wi? be? mbushii? lii? etc.
Ali he? - Where is she? Okholanga shi? - What are you doing?
Uyo niwi? - Who is that person? Bano nibe? - Who are these?
Notsie li? - When will you go? Okhola orio mbushi? - Why do
you do like that?
2. "If" clause.
The 1 is omitted from the ni. In some dialects the remaining n
follows the rules of nasalization, in others the n is almost inaudibly
spoken in the throat.
nibaba nbatsia = mbaba mbatsia, or nbaba nbatsia.
nikuba nkuli = ngube nguli, or nkuba nkuli.
nitsiba nitsili = nziba nzili, or, ntsiba ntsili.
nishiba nishili = nshiba nshili
nibibe nibili = mbiba mbili, or nbiba nbili.
The second forms are found in the Central Duyua area among
others.

5.Verbs ending in -ra in their applied or near and intermediate past tenses:
Pattern: VR + 'ra/'re

tsererere = ts'er're

Ifula yibirile = Ifula yibir're. Mdeerela omukaate. Mdeer'ra

Pattern: SP + VR + itsa'a or, SP + VS + itsa'a (coalesce)
Aliitsa'a = He is eating. Banyweetsa'a = They are drinking.
b.Other verbs not ending in -ia.
Pattern: SP + VS + 'a
Okholange shiina? = Okhola'a shi? - What are you doing?
Conjunctives
A conjunction is a connecting word or particle used to join words, groups of words, and clauses in sentences. There are two main types of conjunctives: Co-ordinating and Subordinating.
Co-ordinating conjunctions connect things of equal rank: nouns with nouns, adjectives with adjectives, verbs with verbs, phrases with phrases, and clauses with clauses.
Subordinating conjunctions connect a subordinate clause with a word or another clause on which it depends.
1.Co-ordinating conjunctions may be divided into four groups:
a. Addition
nende - and
khandi - and, also, furthermore
ne - and
ali...ali - both, included
b. Choice
nohomba...nohomba - (n)either...
(n)or *
noho, nohomba, kata...kata -
(n)either...(n)or *
* With positive construction these word combinations mean "either..." or, and with negative construction, "neither...nor."
c. Contrast
nabutswa - but
ne - but, nevertheless
kata - even, even though,
habula - except, but
d. Inference or Reason
khulwa mbu - because of, for the reason that
khulveko - because of this/that
eshichila ni - the reason being
kho - so, well then, so that,
therefore
okhuba - for, because, being
shichila - because, the reason being
2. Subordinating conjunctions may be divided into five groups.
a. Purpose
mbu - that, so that, in order that
khulwa - for, because of
kho - in order that
mbu,-ri - introduce direct speech,
lists of things, or something
specific

Word Order
The foundation of the Luyia sentence is the noun which is the
subject of the sentence. This noun dominates the sentence, and all
words related to it are brought into concordial agreement by
prefixes and suffixes.
1. The normal word order in a Luyia sentence is: subject, predicate
or verb, indirect object, direct object.
Omundu sheetsanga omukhasi omukaate. - The man is giving the woman
some bread.
2. For emphasis the object may come first, using the object prefix.
Emisazala chino, enjirimanga. - These trees, I am chopping them down.
3. Qualificatives, i.e., adjectives, demonstratives, possessives, numbers, ideophones, etc., follow the words they modify. Usually possessives come first. Bull and shea are exceptions; they precede the words they qualify.
Abana banje bano bataru nabakali. - These three children of
mine are large.
If the qualificative referring to the noun might be confused with a following noun, the qualificative may precede the possessive.
Omwana uno owmukhasi uyo nomulwale. - This child of that woman
is ill.
Adjectives or adverbs modifying the same word may or may not require a conjunction. The conjunction used would be khandi.
Omundu uno nemulayi omukhongoi or, omundu uno nomulayi khandi
nomukhongo. - This person is good and large.
4. Order of prefixes. shi + SP; SP + re; OP + VS;
SP + ra + tense prefix + OP + VS; or, SP + tense prefix + OP + VS
Abana abakhakumhoonye, mbabano. - These are the children who
will help her.
Abarasakhatsie ta, mbabo. - There are those who will not go.
5. Adverbs of time may come first, last, or follow the noun subject
and its qualificatives in a sentence.
Leelo abandu bano balimanga; or, abandu balimanga leelo; or, abandu bano leelo balimanga. - These people are digging today, etc.
6. With the applied form of the verb the indirect object comes first,
then the direct object.
Omsaatsa aboolela omukhasi amakhwa amatinyu. - The man is saying
hard words to the woman.
7. Adverbial interrogatives: shiina? - rie? mbushina? liina? heena?
wine? beena? banga? etc., usually come at the end of the sentence
or clause in which they appear. Mbushina may come first, and when
it does, it is often followed by ni construction of the verb.
Nakhusitse liina? - When shall we go?
Atsitsaanga bulano mbushina? - Why is he going now? or,
Mbushina naratsia bulaano ta? - Why is he not going now?

- 180 -
Relationship Terms
The European unit of social life is the family. The African unit is the clan. Their relationship terms indicate the inter-relationship which exists within the clan. No one Luyia relationship corresponds exactly with the European family relationship.
Kinship terms are an important part of many legal situations, particularly cases in court. So it is well to know something of these terms for practical purposes, as well as to have an idea of basic problems of the emerging Luyia society today.
1.Eshisoni = great-grandfather, great-grandmother (rather vague)
2.Kuuka = grandfather;kuukayo;kuukanyene;kuuka weenywe/wabwe
Kuukhu = grandmother;nyakukhulu;nyakukhulunyene;kuukhu weefwe,etc.
3.Papa = father, any of father's brothers, or brothers of maternal
Paternal uncles sometimes: papa wakhabili.
Aunts
Mama = mother, father's other wives,mother's sisters, and father's
brother's wives. All except one's own mother are often
called: mama wakhabili. But the child always addresses them
as "mama," and the men "papa."
4.Senje = father's sister, paternal aunt.
Senjenyene = his/her paternal aunt.
Senjenyene Luka = Luke's paternal aunt.
5.Khotsa = mother's brother, maternal uncle.
Khotsanyene = his/her maternal uncle
Khotsanyene Sara = Sarah's maternal uncle
6.Omwana wanje, omwana weefwe = my/our child; spoken of any child
In the clan of the same generation as one's own children.
Also omwana weefwe
can refer to brothers,sisters or
cousins - those of one's own generation in the clan.
7.Omwana weenywe = your child, or your brother/sister,cousin or any
one of one's own generation in the clan.
8.Omwana wabwe = their brother/sister,child,cousin, or anyone of
their own generation in the clan.
The plurals of these last three are:abaana banje, abaana beefwe,
abaana beenywe, abaana babwe.
Shorter forms are: omwananje,omwaneefwe,omwaneenywe,omwanabwe.
Other forms are: oewefwe, oweenywe, ovaabwe;absawefwe,abaawenywe,
absawabwe.
9.Nyina = the mother, his/her mother.
Nyinamwana = his/her mother
Nyinamwana Omwakwe = Omwakwe's mother
Mamavo = your mother (s.) The old form mavo is very much objected
to by the young people of today.
Mama, or nyineefwe = our mother, term of address to mother-in-law
is: Mame.
Nyineenywe = your (pl.) mother
Nyinaabwe = their mother; Abaa= is prefixed to all nyina-forms for
plural.
10.Samwana = his/her father, the child's father.
Samwana Yohana = John's father.
Paps, seefwe = our father; Paps = term of address to one's fatherin-law
; also Kuuka.
Seenywe = your (pl.) father.
Sabwe = their father.
Samwana abaana -Rita nende Yohana - Rita's and John's father.
Samwana abaana = their father.
Abas= may be prefixed to paps or the sa terms for plural.
11.Omusesnjetsanwa = what children's senje calls them.
12.Omwiha, abeehwa = what children's khotsa calls them.
13.Omwitsukhulu = grandchild
14.Nufiala = what the children of khotsa and senje call each other.
15.Abeinzu/inyumba = the nearest one can get to "family."

Abeinzu yeefwe - our family, ones of our house.
16.Mbotswa - 'my brother (if female speaking);my sister (if male is
    baije
Abambotswey brothers/sisters;said of opposite sex.
Mbotsoyd, your brother/sister;your brothers(to girl-s),your sise
Ababotsoyo/beenywe - plural for the above. ter-s (to boy-s)
Mbotsonyene - his sister,her brother.
Mbotsonyene Rita/Yohana - Rita's brother,John's sister.
Abaambotsonyene,abambotswo wabwe - their brothers/sisters.
17.Omukhaana weefwe - my/our sister;abakhaana beeefwe - my/our sisters.
Omukhaana weenye - your sister;abakhaana beenywe - your sisters.
Omukhaana waawe - his/her/sister.
Omukhaana wanga - his/her sister.
Omukhaana wanga Festo/Rita - Festo's or Rita's sister.
The plurals for all these would be aba,ba-.
The terms for brother/brothers are the same as above, except the
words.omusieni and abesiani are substituted for omukhaans and
abakhaands.
By the terms."brother(s)" and "sister(s)" we mean all of one's
own generation in a clan,-clan brothers and sisters, i.e.,brothers, sisters, cousins.
18.Omusaatsa wanje, omwami wanje - my-husband;omuseankhulu wanje,
Omwenemuchitsi,omwenemulwanyi - the husband of a home,
Mukha Yohana - John's wife
19.Omukhasi wanje,omuteeshi wanje,omuchiehele wanje (respect) - my
Omwenenzu,omwenenyumba - the wife of a home,
/wife.
Omukhasi omkholundu/wakhabili/wakhataru,etc. - first/second/
third wife,etc, of a polygamist.
Omukhaye - a favorite wife, lady, wife of a monogamist,-a very
.fine woman.
Muhalikhwa - what polygamist's wives call each other.
20.Mafiala - my mother-in-law,Nyakhufialasyenyakhufialanyene,etc.
These are used when speaking of the mother-in-law. In
direct address one says, "Mama."
A mother-in-law Also uses these terms when referring
to a son-in-law or daughter-in-law. But in direct
address she says,"Omusiani/omukhaana wanje/wo,"etc.
The same is true of the father-in-law,toward a sonin-law
or daughter-in-law.
21.Papa, kuuka - one's father-in-law.
22.Mulamwa - what a woman and her husband's brother/cousin call
each other;also a man and his wife's sister/cousin call
each other;a man and his brother's wife call each other
this;also, a woman and her husband's sister's husband;
a man and his wife's brother's wife. Remember "brother"
and 'sister" always refer to the term "cousin "-also.
23.Omukhawi wanje,omukhwe wanje - the term which the following
call each other;a man and his wife's brother/cousin;a
man and his sister's/cousin husband.
24.Muhalikhwa - what a woman and her husband's brother's/cousin's
wife call each other.
25.Massakwa - what a man and his wife's sister's/cousin's husband
call each other.
Each wife has her own separate house and garden, and the children of
one wife are called abomunzu ndala,abeinzu/inyumba-ndala - ones of
one house (another possible term for "family). Children of one man,
by all his wives, can be called omusaatsa mulala. The nearest
to the English "brothers and sisters" is abomukhasi mulala.
A clan (oluya) are the descendants of one man and may not intermarry.
The Luyia society is patrilineal;the children belong to the father's
clan. When a girl marries,she is lost to the clan.That is the reason
for the ikhwe-downry an equilibrium guarantee.Such a girl is called
omukoko. The clan name for abakoko is inohe.
